nodes.title: Replace the existing flat graph with one richly-typed rebuild
nodes.description: Wipe the 106 nodes (10 goals + 96 observations, no options/decisions/actions/outcomes) and rebuild the book as a single canonical-flow graph. One description of each lesson, at the cost of losing the earlier pass.

nodes.title: Keep the flat graph and layer the new flow on top
nodes.description: Leave all 106 existing nodes in place and add the flow, theme and AI_NOTE layers alongside them. Preserves the earlier pass but leaves two overlapping descriptions of the same 8 lessons in one graph.

nodes.title: Build the new graph in a separate deciduous directory
nodes.description: Keep the root graph untouched and build into exploration/.deciduous/. Non-destructive, but splits the repo across two graphs and diverges from the single-graph workflow in CLAUDE.md.

nodes.title: Rebuild the graph from scratch, after backing up the database
nodes.description: User chose the clean rebuild. The existing graph was a flat lesson dump with no options, decisions, actions or outcomes, so it could not support the flow the exploration site renders. Backed up to .deciduous/backups and to the session scratchpad before wiping; the source PDF attachment was repointed to the new root goal rather than lost.

nodes.title: Put the exploration site at site/public/exploration/
nodes.description: site/ is already the Next.js course app here, unlike tim_blausey where site/index.html IS the explorer. Serving the explorer from the Next app's public directory means it ships with the course at /exploration and shares its warm palette.

nodes.title: Read the book in 11 parallel passes and assemble the graph via a workflow
nodes.description: 16-agent workflow: one reader per unit (front matter + design spec, lessons 1-8, closing overview), then a synthesis barrier producing themes, the book-level spine and cross-lesson arcs, and the alignment between the design prompt's expressed goals and the lesson content, then a commentary pass emitting AI_NOTE nodes. Every content node is required to carry verbatim quotes from the source.

nodes.title: Build the exploration site as a standalone page in the course app's public directory
nodes.description: Single-file d3 explorer with six views: overview with the book spine, force-directed flow graph with per-unit and per-type filters and an AI-notes toggle, a lesson-by-lesson reading view, theme cards, the AI commentary layer, and search. Palette taken from the course app's own tokens (warm white, soft grey, muted natural accents) rather than copied from the tim_blausey explorer.

nodes.title: Point this project at the shared OpenAI key
nodes.description: Reused the same OPEN_AI_API_KEY as tim_blausey via a local .env, and added .env to .gitignore here so the key is not committed.

nodes.title: Parents arrive frustrated and overwhelmed by strategies too clinical for real life
nodes.description:
The preface opens by naming the reader's state rather than the subject matter: frustration, uncertainty about what the child is trying to communicate, and exhaustion from advice that does not survive contact with a real household. Lolly generalizes this from years spent alongside families, framing the problem as a mismatch between available strategies and daily life rather than any failing of the parent. This premise is the thing every later promise answers. The separate design prompt restates the same premise as a constraint on the website itself, which is why the framing layer spans both documents.

Sources:
- "Parents who care deeply, who are trying everything they can, and who are often left feeling overwhelmed by strategies that are either too complicated, too clinical, or just don’t fit into real life."
- "Parents using this course may already be overwhelmed. The website should reduce cognitive load, not add to it."

nodes.title: Parent uses simple visual supports at home to reduce frustration and build communication
nodes.description:
The book's top-level goal is stated as a capability the parent will have, not knowledge they will hold: using visual supports inside their own home. Three results are named together as the target state, reduced frustration, supported independence, and meaningful communication. The promise is explicitly pitched at any starting point, whether the parent is new to visuals or already using some. Everything downstream, the eight lessons, the printables, and the website design, exists to deliver this one capability.

Sources:
- "In Say It With Pictures, you’ll learn how to use simple, effective visual supports at home to reduce frustration, support independence, and build meaningful communication."
- "Whether you’re just starting out or looking to strengthen what’s already working, this course is designed to meet you where you are."

nodes.title: Give parents more theory and another long list of strategies to try
nodes.description:
The preface names the conventional approach it is refusing before it describes its own. More theory and longer lists of things to try are treated as the default the field already offers and as part of why parents feel defeated. The text also sets aside the idea that the parent must first become a credentialed helper, a variant of the same load-adding path. It is raised only to be dismissed, which is what makes it an option rather than a premise.

Sources:
- "What they need isn’t more theory."
- "They don’t need another long list of things to try."
- "You don’t need to be a therapist, a teacher, or a behaviour expert to help your child learn to communicate."

nodes.title: Give parents something real and practical they can use today
nodes.description:
The alternative path is defined by immediacy and fit: real, practical, usable the same day. Its credibility rests on provenance rather than citation, the material is described as built from hands-on years and shaped by actual homes and daily challenges. The promised contents are concrete objects rather than concepts: modules, printables, cheat sheets, examples. This is the path the book commits to.

Sources:
- "They need something real. Practical. Something they can use today."
- "Everything you’ll find here is built from those years of hands-on experience, shaped by real families, real homes, and real daily challenges."
- "Printable visual tools you can start using right away"

nodes.title: Decide what an overwhelmed parent actually needs from a course
nodes.description:
The preface stages an explicit choice between two named alternatives, theory and long lists versus something usable today, and resolves it in a single line. The resolution is given as the reason the course exists at all. The choice is justified by experience of both sides, what works and what does not, rather than by literature. Everything about the course's structure follows from landing on the practical side of this choice.

Sources:
- "That’s why I created this course."
- "I’ve seen what works, and what doesn’t."

nodes.title: Author's authority claim: 25 years, a centre founded at 20, 1,000+ families, mother of three
nodes.description:
The authority claim is built in three layers. Professional length and scale come first, over 25 years as teacher and behaviour specialist and a treatment centre serving more than a thousand families. Institutional specificity follows, a named organization founded at age 20 and operating in the Greater Toronto Area since 2002. Then a personal layer is added, parenting three children, which lets the author claim the overwhelm she describes rather than only observing it.

Sources:
- "With over 25 years of experience as a teacher, behaviour specialist, and founder of a full-service behavioural treatment centre supporting more than 1,000 children with autism and their families, I’ve seen what works, and what doesn’t."
- "Lolly Herman is the founder and Executive Director of Under the Umbrella Tree Educational Services (UTUT), a behavioural treatment centre for children with disabilities that she launched at just 20 years old."
- "As a mother of three, Lolly understands firsthand how overwhelming it can feel to balance it all, especially when a child struggles to communicate their needs."

nodes.title: Working model of autism: the clinical definition, cited then deliberately held at arm's length
nodes.description:
The primer adopts a single sourced definition of ASD as a neurodevelopmental condition with deficits in social interaction and communication plus restricted, repetitive behaviour. Immediately after citing it, the book distances itself from the clinical register, saying those words do not describe daily life for the child or the family. The parent is explicitly released from needing diagnostic expertise. The definition is therefore kept as scaffolding for the strategies, not as content the parent must master.

Sources:
- "autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by significant deficits in social interaction, communication, and patterns of behaviour that are restricted and repetitive in nature"
- "But those clinical words don’t always reflect what day-to-day life looks like for a child with autism, or for the people who love them."
- "You don’t need to become an expert in diagnosis."

nodes.title: Social communication differences mean non-verbal behaviour carries much of the message
nodes.description:
The first of two named areas where autism shows up in daily life is the back-and-forth rhythm of communication. The book lists observable surface signs, initiating and responding, gestures and eye contact, tone and abstract language, preference for non-social routines. The load-bearing inference is that a child may be expressing needs through non-verbal behaviour, which relocates the work onto the adult. The caregiver's job becomes observing and reinforcing efforts that are already happening.

Sources:
- "Children with autism may struggle with the back-and-forth rhythm of typical communication."
- "children with autism may also rely more on non-verbal behaviour to express needs, making it especially important that caregivers become skilled at observing and reinforcing these efforts"

nodes.title: Repetitive and restrictive behaviours are coping and comfort, not problems to fix
nodes.description:
The second named area covers repeated phrases or actions, need for routine and sameness, deep focused interests, and sensory sensitivities. The book takes an explicit stance against treating these as targets for elimination. It reframes them functionally, as coping, sensory-seeking, or expressions of interest, and argues that understanding purpose is what enables support. This reframing licenses the course's later emphasis on predictability and routine rather than on suppression.

Sources:
- "These behaviours aren’t problems to be “fixed.”"
- "They are often coping strategies, sensory-seeking actions, or expressions of interest and comfort. When we understand their purpose, we can better support the child behind them."

nodes.title: Core premise: children with autism often learn best through visual, structured, hands-on supports
nodes.description:
This is the hinge that connects the autism primer to the rest of the course, and it is the justification for a course about pictures specifically. Learning is said to go best when it is consistent, structured, visual, and hands-on. Alongside it the book names the mechanisms it will use, prompting, reinforcement, and environmental design. The stated payoff is clarity and predictability, which reduce frustration for the parent as well as the child.

Sources:
- "Children with autism often learn best through consistent, structured, visual, and hands-on supports."
- "promoting skill generalization and building meaningful communication involves strategic prompting, reinforcement, and environmental design, all of which you’ll find throughout this course's Preface"
- "Reduce frustration (for both of you) by increasing clarity and predictability"

nodes.title: Build every lesson on the same seven-part shape, Read and Learn through Let's Keep Going
nodes.description:
The course answers the practical-over-theoretical choice with a fixed repeating container for every lesson. The seven parts run from bite-sized teaching, to reflection, to examples from other families, to a parent activity, then the optional extension workbook and community discussion, and finally a forward-looking recap. Two of the seven are explicitly optional, which keeps the core path small. The shape is designed to work the same whether the parent studies alone or with others.

Sources:
- "Whether you're doing it solo or with others, each lesson follows the same core structure:"
- "Each lesson offers bite-sized learning, simple activities, and real-life examples you can use right away."
- "At the end of each lesson, we’ll take a moment to reflect on what you’ve explored and look ahead to what’s coming next."

nodes.title: Let parents move at their own pace and revisit lessons, with an optional community alongside
nodes.description:
Rather than pacing the course, the book hands pacing to the parent and states that lessons can be revisited as needed. Community is offered as a genuine add-on, not a requirement, on the explicit grounds that everything necessary is already in the course. The framing closes the preface on companionship rather than obligation. This same commitment reappears in the design prompt as a rule that completed lessons must never be locked.

Sources:
- "You can move through it at your own pace, revisiting lessons as needed."
- "While everything you need is right here in this course, some families enjoy learning alongside others."
- "Do not lock completed lessons. Parents should be able to revisit anything at any time."

nodes.title: Promised result: a home set up for communication, less frustration, connection restored
nodes.description:
The preface predicts the payoff in terms of the whole household, not just the child's skills. A home intentionally arranged to support communication is described as transformative, especially for a child who does not yet use words. The benefit is deliberately extended to the parent, the family, and a connection framed as currently missing. This is the outcome the framing layer promises and the eight lessons are meant to produce.

Sources:
- "Because when a home is intentionally set up to support communication, especially for a child who doesn’t yet use words, it can be transformative."
- "For you. For your family. For the connection that’s been missing."

nodes.title: Parent steps into the role of their child's communication detective
nodes.description:
The primer ends by naming the role the parent is being recruited into and handing off directly to Lesson 1. The qualification is a stance rather than knowledge: open, curious, ready to notice. The preface plants the same phrase earlier, tying close observation of the child to growing confidence. This is the immediate deliverable of the framing layer, the mindset the rest of the course is built on top of.

Sources:
- "You just need to be open, curious, and ready to notice. And that’s exactly what you’ll start doing in Lesson 1, as you step into your new role as your child’s communication detective"
- "As you observe your child more closely, you’ll begin to notice and understand their unique communication, becoming a confident “communication detective” along the way."

nodes.title: The course experience should feel warm, calm, grounded, spacious, practical, easy to return to
nodes.description:
The design prompt states the target feeling as six words before it specifies a single screen, making tone the governing requirement. It then translates that feeling into visual instructions: muted natural tones, breathing room, soft typography, minimal clutter, short sections instead of large text blocks. The prompt also anchors the look to an existing sibling property so the course reads as part of the same family. Every layout decision in the document is downstream of this stated feeling.

Sources:
- "Warm. Calm. Grounded. Spacious. Practical. Easy to return to."
- "Create the online course experience for Say It With Pictures so that it feels visually and emotionally connected to the RootedInGood™ website."
- "short sections rather than large blocks of text"

nodes.title: The website should reduce the already-overwhelmed parent's cognitive load, not add to it
nodes.description:
The design prompt carries the preface's premise about overwhelmed parents into a hard requirement on the interface. Reducing cognitive load is stated as the direction of effect, with adding to it named as the failure. Concrete consequences are spelled out: consistency so parents learn the course quickly, and never having to hammer the browser back button to work out where they are. It is the operational half of the warm-and-calm goal.

Sources:
- "Parents using this course may already be overwhelmed. The website should reduce cognitive load, not add to it."
- "Consistency is important because parents should quickly learn how the course works."
- "A parent should never need to use the browser's Back button repeatedly to figure out where they are."

nodes.title: Build it like an LMS or school portal, institutional, medical, worksheet-heavy
nodes.description:
The design prompt enumerates the shapes the experience must not take, and they cluster into one recognisable product: the standard online-school portal with a clinical skin. The list runs institutional, medical, overly colourful, childlike, busy, worksheet-heavy, like an LMS or school portal. A related failure is named separately, the sensation of having opened a very long manual, which is exactly what a 137-page course risks feeling like. Even the imagery is constrained away from this register.

Sources:
- "This is a parent education course, not a clinical learning portal and not a traditional online school."
- "like an LMS or school portal"
- "like the parent has opened a 150-page manual"

nodes.title: Drive completion with points, badges, trophies and streaks
nodes.description:
Gamification is raised as the obvious mechanism for keeping learners moving and then ruled out by name. The prompt still wants completion marked, but the acknowledgement is to be plain and warm rather than scored. A parallel restraint applies to the family stories, which must stay relatable and must not be framed as guaranteed results. Both refusals protect a parent who is already carrying enough pressure from being ranked against a target.

Sources:
- "Avoid gamification such as points, badges, trophies or streaks."
- "Acknowledge progress simply and warmly."
- "Do not present examples as promises of outcomes."

nodes.title: Make the whole thing feel like Lolly gently walking alongside the parent
nodes.description:
The endorsed model for the experience is companionship, stated as a single sentence about how the course should feel. It matches the preface's own closing voice, where the author promises to be present at each week and each lesson. In the interface this becomes supportive callouts carrying Lolly's practical interpretation, plus a reflection section that explicitly asks nothing of the parent. The callouts are required to be useful rather than ornamental.

Sources:
- "The experience should feel like Lolly is gently walking alongside the parent through the course."
- "I’ll be right here with you, each week, each lesson, each step."
- "Nothing needs to be fixed right now. This is a moment to notice."

nodes.title: Decide what kind of learning experience this course should be
nodes.description:
The design prompt makes the category choice before any layout choice, defining the product by what it is not and then by what it should feel like. A clinical learning portal and a traditional online school are both excluded, along with gamified completion mechanics. What is chosen in their place is a companion experience the parent can leave and come back to. The prompt states the acceptance test directly: not something to get through, but something to keep using.

Sources:
- "The course should not feel like something a parent has to “get through.”"
- "It should feel like a resource they can learn from, leave, return to, and keep using."

nodes.title: Build a Course Home that answers where was I, what is done, and what comes next
nodes.description:
The chosen companion model is implemented first as a re-entry point. Course Home must immediately answer the returning parent's four questions, then show progress out of eight lessons, a large Continue Learning card for the next one, and a grid of all eight with status and a start, continue or revisit button. Signing back in lands the parent here rather than wherever they last were. Persistent navigation across Course Home, My Lessons, My Tools and Community keeps that orientation available everywhere.

Sources:
- "Where was I? What have I completed? What comes next? How do I get back to something I found helpful?"
- "When a parent signs back in, take them to the Course Home rather than dropping them randomly into the last page."
- "Keep this navigation simple and consistent."

nodes.title: Collect every printable into a My Tools area organized by category, not by lesson
nodes.description:
The second implementation of the companion model is a standing library so the parent never has to recall which lesson held a given template. Tools are grouped by the job to be done, communication, routines and transitions, independence, preparing for change, with the teaching lesson noted on each card. This inverts the usual course structure, where resources stay buried in the module that introduced them. The design prompt explicitly intends this area to outlive the course itself.

Sources:
- "This should collect the practical resources from the course in one location so parents do not have to remember which lesson contained them."
- "Organize tools by category rather than only by lesson."
- "This section should become something parents continue returning to even after they finish the course."

nodes.title: At any point the parent can say where they are, what to try, and where to find it again
nodes.description:
The design prompt states its success condition as four questions the parent must always be able to answer. Meeting it is what turns a 137-page manual into something re-enterable. The mobile rules are part of the same outcome, since phones are expected to be the main device and progress must stay visible without pinching and zooming. The measure of success is continued use after completion rather than completion itself.

Sources:
- "Where am I?"
- "Where can I find this again later?"
- "Design mobile-first."

nodes.title: Lesson 1 goal: see your child's communication differently and make home the place it works
nodes.description:
Lesson 1's stated aim is a shift in the parent's perception rather than a new workload: notice the small communicative moments that get missed and understand how the home environment shapes the child's success. The lesson frames the home as the child's best classroom and positions everything that follows (generalization, prompting, visual supports) as ways to make everyday moments calmer and more connected. It is explicitly not a "do more" lesson but a "see differently" lesson, which is why its only required task is observation.

Sources:
- "In this first lesson, we’re going to shift how you see your child’s world and how they communicate within it."
- "This isn’t about doing more. It’s about seeing differently and using that understanding to create calmer, more connected everyday moments."

nodes.title: Opening vignette: the 4:45 p.m. fridge meltdown and the same moment weeks later
nodes.description:
The lesson opens with a composite scene a parent is meant to recognize: late afternoon, a crying child at the fridge, four rejected snacks, and a parent who cannot decode the request. The author names the real pain as not understanding one's own child rather than the snack itself. She then replays the identical scene weeks later with a visual choice board on the fridge door, and the child pointing to yogurt. This before/after pair is the emotional premise that sets up the whole lesson.

Sources:
- "You’re in the kitchen. It’s 4:45 p.m. Your child is standing in front of the fridge, crying."
- "This moment isn’t just about snacks; it’s about the feeling of not understanding your own child."
- "Same child. Same fridge. No meltdown."

nodes.title: Keep listening mainly for spoken words as the measure of communication
nodes.description:
The lesson names, in order to set aside, the default stance most parents arrive with: treating speech as the thing to watch for, because that is what we were taught to look for. Its consequence is the false conclusion that a child who is not yet talking is not communicating. The book treats this as understandable but factually wrong, and corrects it directly.

Sources:
- "But many parents (understandably!) focus mainly on spoken language, because that’s what we’ve been taught to look for."
- "So it can feel like a child who isn’t talking yet isn’t communicating. That’s not true."

nodes.title: Become a communication detective and read the non-verbal signals already there
nodes.description:
The alternative the lesson offers is to widen what counts as communication: gestures, facial expressions, body language, vocal tone, visual attention, sounds, pictures and actions. It grounds this in the claim that the large majority of communication is non-verbal, so the child's signals already exist and only need noticing. The parent's role is reframed from teacher-of-speech to detective tuning into signals that are subtle but meaningful.

Sources:
- "Here’s something most people don’t realize: Over 90% of communication is non-verbal."
- "Some children use words, while others use gestures, sounds, facial expressions, pictures, or actions to share what they need."
- "Think of yourself as a communication detective, someone who’s about to discover a whole new way of understanding their child."

nodes.title: Choose to read all behaviour as communication instead of waiting for speech
nodes.description:
The lesson makes the choice for the parent and states it plainly: the child is already communicating, so the open question is whether the adult is noticing. It backs the choice with a definitional move borrowed from behaviour analysis, where behaviour means anything a person does, including stillness, not just problem behaviour. Adopting this lens is what makes every later tool legible, because a point at a card is now a message rather than a non-answer.

Sources:
- "Your child is already communicating. The question is, are we noticing what they’re telling us?"
- "In the field of behaviour analysis, behaviour simply means anything a person does, including communication, gestures, choices, movements, and even stillness."
- "Understanding all behaviour (not just “bad” behaviour) helps us see how a child is communicating, coping, or asking for help, even if they don’t yet have the words."

nodes.title: Generalization: using a learned skill in a new setting is a core autism challenge
nodes.description:
The lesson's central teaching concept is generalization, defined as carrying a skill from where it was taught into other settings, people and moments, without relearning it. It illustrates the failure case with a child who requests a bathroom break at school using a card, a raised hand and a specific door, but does not ask at home where none of those cues exist. The book attributes this to heavy reliance on specific cues and to the flexibility that generalization demands, not to effort or misbehaviour.

Sources:
- "Generalization is the ability to take a skill learned in one setting, like therapy or school, and use it in another, like at home, on the playground, or with a sibling."
- "Imagine this: Your child learns how to request a bathroom break with their educational assistant at school."
- "That’s why generalization is considered a core challenge in autism. It requires something that’s often hard for autistic learners: flexibility."

nodes.title: Get therapy and school skills showing up at home, with siblings, and in the community
nodes.description:
Having defined generalization, the lesson sets the working goal of the whole course: bring the skills the child already has into the home and other everyday settings. Its promise is that generalization is teachable and supportable rather than something to wait for. Success looks like the crackers moment, where a child spontaneously signals "help" at home after learning it in therapy.

Sources:
- "Stories like this are incredibly common, and that’s why this course focuses so much on helping you bring skills into your home."
- "But here’s the good news: We can teach it. We can support it."
- "It’s when something your child learned in one place starts showing up in real life, at home, at the park, with grandparents, or with a sibling."

nodes.title: Put the four supports in place: consistency, collaboration, practice in many settings, modelling
nodes.description:
The lesson names four conditions that make generalization more likely and presents them together rather than as competing choices. Consistency means the same language, visuals and cues across environments; collaboration means parents, teachers and therapists using similar tools and expectations; practice means repeating the skill at home, school and in the community; modelling means demonstrating the request or choice so the child can imitate it. These four are the concrete content behind the lesson's advice to build consistency, use visual tools, and practise in different settings with different people.

Sources:
- "Children are more likely to generalize skills when certain supports are in place."
- "Consistency- Using the same language, visuals, and cues across environments helps reduce confusion and builds confidence."
- "Collaboration- When parents, teachers, and therapists use similar tools and expectations, your child is more likely to carry skills between settings."

nodes.title: Read the missing skill at home as regression, lost progress, or a behaviour problem
nodes.description:
The lesson surfaces the interpretation parents commonly reach for when a skill appears in therapy but not at dinner: that the child has gone backwards, or is choosing not to comply. It rejects this reading on three grounds, saying it is not regression, not effort, and not behaviour, but a difference in how information is processed and cues are recognized. Naming this misreading matters because it is what makes parents feel they are doing something wrong.

Sources:
- "This isn’t regression. It’s simply a sign that generalization hasn’t happened yet."
- "It’s also why you might feel like your child is making progress in one place, only to “lose” that progress somewhere else."
- "It’s not about effort. It’s not about behaviour. It’s about how their brains process information."

nodes.title: Change the environment rather than the verdict on the child
nodes.description:
Faced with a skill that does not transfer, the lesson tells the parent to act on the setting instead of concluding something about the child. The chosen route is consistency across environments, visual tools, and practice with different people and places; the discarded route is the regression reading. The book's own summary of the mother-and-daughter case states the causal claim directly: the result changed because the environment was set up to support success.

Sources:
- "And we can make it easier by building consistency across environments, using visual tools, and practicing in different settings with different people."
- "Same child. Different setting. Different result, because the environment was now set up to support her success."

nodes.title: Put a visual choice board on the fridge and use it exactly the way therapy does
nodes.description:
The lesson's first concrete tool is a visual choice board placed where the need arises, with the fridge door as the worked example. Crucially, the instruction is not just to hang the board but to practise with it the same way the therapist does, which is the consistency support made physical. The board gives the child a way to answer the snack question by pointing instead of escalating.

Sources:
- "Once we put a visual choice board on the fridge and practiced using it the same way they did in therapy, things started to shift."
- "Your child walks to the fridge. There’s a visual choice board on the door. They point to a picture of yogurt."

nodes.title: Story: the mom whose daughter was "a rockstar in therapy" but showed none of it at home
nodes.description:
The author recounts a mother she worked with whose daughter used picture cards, followed instructions and made vocal requests in therapy, yet did none of it at home. The mother read this as her own failure. The author's reframe is that the skills simply had not generalized and the daughter needed help connecting the dots between settings. This vignette is the lesson's bridge from the concept of generalization to the choice-board intervention.

Sources:
- "A mom I worked with once told me, “My daughter is a rockstar in therapy. She can use her picture cards, follow instructions, and even ask for things with her voice. But when we get home, none of it happens.”"
- "She felt discouraged, like she was doing something wrong. But the truth was, her daughter hadn’t yet generalized those skills."

nodes.title: The daughter moved from pointing to choosing to requesting across both settings
nodes.description:
After the fridge board went up and was used the same way as in therapy, the book reports a graded change rather than an overnight one: pointing first, then choosing, then requesting, and eventually the same skills in both therapy and home. The sequence is offered as what environmental consistency actually buys a family. It is the lesson's proof case that generalization can be engineered.

Sources:
- "Slowly, her daughter began pointing. Then choosing and then requesting. And eventually, using the same skills across both settings."
- "If this story feels familiar to you, you’re in the right place."

nodes.title: Help enough that the child succeeds, little enough that independence grows
nodes.description:
Once the board is on the fridge, a new problem appears: the child approaches, sees it, and freezes. The lesson's second goal is to give help that produces success now without the parent permanently doing the work. It states the balance explicitly as the right amount of help at the right time, then reduced, and uses training wheels as the image for temporary support aimed at independence.

Sources:
- "Using the Prompting Hierarchy: Helping Without Taking Over"
- "The goal isn’t to avoid prompting; it’s to give the right amount of help at the right time, and then slowly reduce it as your child becomes more confident."
- "Think of it like training wheels. You’re there to steady them while they’re learning, but the long-term goal is for them to ride on their own."

nodes.title: The Prompting Hierarchy: independent, model, gesture, partial physical, full physical
nodes.description:
The lesson's signature tool is a five-level ladder of support running from independent performance at the top, through model and gesture, to partial physical and full hand-over-hand guidance at the base. The parent starts at whatever level the child needs and works upward toward independence. The book is emphatic that the ladder is a flexible framework, not a fixed order, and that the starting point and pacing vary by child, skill and context.

Sources:
- "The Prompting Hierarchy is a simple, step-by-step way to help your child learn a new skill, while gently guiding them toward independence and limiting or removing the prompt."
- "Here are the five levels of the Prompting Hierarchy, from most independent to most supportive:"
- "The prompting hierarchy is not a rigid, one-size-fits-all system, but rather a flexible framework that adapts to the individual learner, the specific skill being taught, and the context in which learning occurs."

nodes.title: Errorless teaching: supply enough help up front that the child succeeds first time
nodes.description:
Errorless teaching, also called errorless learning, means front-loading support so the child does not accumulate mistakes or frustration while learning. The parent starts strong and pulls back over time, which builds a clean, repeatable chain the child can rely on. The lesson argues this matters most for children still working out how their actions connect to outcomes, for whom starting with success is the point.

Sources:
- "Errorless teaching means giving your child the right amount of help from the beginning, so they don’t make repeated mistakes or feel stuck and frustrated."
- "This is part of a teaching approach called errorless learning, where you help your child succeed before mistakes happen."
- "You’re building a clear, repeatable chain of behaviours: “When I point, I get.”"

nodes.title: Hold back help, let the child get it wrong, then correct
nodes.description:
The lesson raises the objection a parent is likely to feel, that constant helping will prevent independence, and names the alternative it implies: withhold support, wait for the error, then correct it. It sets this approach aside in favour of errorless teaching, while also guarding the other flank by insisting the recommendation is not over-helping. The concern is that repeated mistakes leave the child stuck and frustrated rather than learning.

Sources:
- "You might be wondering, “If I always help, how will they ever learn to do it on their own?”"
- "Instead of waiting for your child to get it wrong and then correcting them, you start with strong support and slowly pull back over time."
- "It’s not about over-helping."

nodes.title: Start with the support the child needs, then fade it level by level
nodes.description:
The lesson resolves the prompting question by combining the hierarchy with errorless teaching: give help before failure, then systematically reduce it as the child succeeds. The concrete fade path it names runs from guiding the hand, to a point, to a model, to nothing. The parent's judgment sets the entry level and the pace; the direction of travel is always toward independence.

Sources:
- "So at first, you might guide their hand to make a choice. Then you shift to a point. Then a model. Then nothing at all."
- "It’s about giving your child a pathway to feel capable, from the start."
- "What matters most is using your judgment to meet the child where they are, adjusting prompts in real time, and always working toward increasing independence in a way that feels supportive, appropriate, and achievable for each individual."

nodes.title: Run the prompting ladder at the fridge board and step it back as the child succeeds
nodes.description:
The lesson walks the whole hierarchy through one routine. If the child points to yogurt alone, that is independent; if not, model the action and say "I want yogurt"; if they hesitate, gesture at the board; if needed, guide the hand partway; and if still unsure, go hand-over-hand. Next time, the parent opens at the level that worked last time rather than waiting for confusion, and moves up a level once the current prompt produces easy responding. Pacing is set by the child, with some moving in days and others staying at a level for weeks.

Sources:
- "If they still don’t respond, you could model the action: point to yogurt and say, “I want yogurt.”"
- "Since you gave a gesture last time, you can begin by immediately offering the same gesture again without waiting for them to become confused or stuck."
- "Let your child guide the pace. There’s no rush, only steady progress, built on connection and trust."

nodes.title: Each faded prompt builds confidence, independence and communication skills
nodes.description:
The lesson's claimed return on prompt fading is cumulative: every reduction that the child meets successfully adds confidence, independence and communication skill. The endpoint it predicts is a child who needs no help at all with that routine, with the prompt gone and the skill retained. It frames this as something worth deliberately celebrating rather than a quiet milestone.

Sources:
- "Every time you reduce the prompt and your child succeeds, you’re building something bigger:"
- "With each success, their confidence grows and eventually, the prompt fades, but the skill remains."
- "Over time, your child won’t need any help at all."

nodes.title: The skill stops belonging to one moment and travels across people, places and things
nodes.description:
The lesson's headline outcome is a skill that leaves its original teaching context and becomes part of ordinary life, usable with different people, in different rooms, and for different objects. Mateo's word "more" is the worked illustration: from mom at the kitchen table with banana, to dad with bubbles, to grandma at the swing, and from banana to crackers, tickles and swings. The book treats this spread as the signal that learning has genuinely stuck.

Sources:
- "Over time, the word stopped belonging to just one moment and started becoming a tool Mateo could use anywhere."
- "That’s what generalization looks like, when a skill moves beyond the original teaching moment and becomes part of everyday life."
- "That’s when you know the learning is really starting to stick."

nodes.title: Family story: Sasha's son and the three-option snack board
nodes.description:
Sasha's son was overwhelmed every afternoon by the open question of what snack he wanted. Sasha introduced a visual snack board limited to three options and modelled its use for a week, beginning with hand-over-hand prompting and fading to a gesture. He began pointing independently, and the book notes the skill held regardless of who was with him, which it labels generalization across people.

Sources:
- "Sasha’s son would get overwhelmed every afternoon when asked what snack he wanted."
- "They began with hand-over-hand prompting, then faded to just a gesture."
- "Now, snack time is a calm, connected routine regardless of who is with him, eating a snack, generalizing the skill across people."

nodes.title: Family story: Jared's daughter and the matching bathroom picture card
nodes.description:
Jared's daughter could request the bathroom at daycare using a picture card, but had frequent accidents at home. Jared closed the gap by placing the same picture card near the home bathroom door and rehearsing the routine with partial physical prompts. Within a couple of weeks she pointed to the card unaided and the accidents stopped, which the book calls generalization across environments.

Sources:
- "Jared’s daughter had learned to request the bathroom at daycare using a picture card, but at home, she would have frequent accidents."
- "Jared placed the same picture card near the bathroom door and practiced the routine with partial physical prompts at first."
- "Within a couple of weeks, she started pointing to the card on her own, no more accidents."

nodes.title: Family story: Anika's 5-year-old learning to put on her shoes
nodes.description:
Anika's five-year-old struggled with the steps of putting on her shoes. Anika applied the prompting strategy, starting with a model and then light hand guidance at the partial physical level, and marked each small success. The child ended up managing her shoes with only a little verbal encouragement, illustrating prompt fading inside a self-care routine rather than a communication one.

Sources:
- "Anika’s 5-year-old was learning to put on her shoes."
- "She struggled with the steps until Anika began using a prompting strategy, first showing (model), then lightly guiding her hands (partial physical)."
- "Anika celebrated each small success, and eventually her daughter was able to put on her shoes with just a little verbal encouragement."

nodes.title: Family story: Mateo's word "more" spreading across people, places and things
nodes.description:
Mateo first used "more" only at snack time with his mom, practised over many repetitions with pieces of banana at the kitchen table. Over the following weeks the family deliberately rehearsed the same word in new situations: dad with bubbles, grandmother at the swing, the living room, the park, and objects beyond banana. The story is the book's three-axis demonstration of generalization across people, places and things.

Sources:
- "When Mateo first learned to say “more”, he only used the word during snack time with his mom."
- "Across people: Mateo first said “more” with Mom. Later, Dad encouraged him to say “more” when they were playing with bubbles."
- "Across things: In the beginning, “more” meant more banana. Soon it also meant more crackers, more bubbles, more tickles, and more swings."

nodes.title: Parent activity: spend 10-15 minutes observing your home with the Generalization Checklist
nodes.description:
The lesson's only required task is observation, not change. In the Pause and Reflect step the parent completes the Generalization Checklist worksheet, then the Parent Activity asks for 10 to 15 minutes observing the home using the Self-Assessment Generalization Checklist. The three stated purposes are to identify where generalization is already happening, spot where added structure would help, and start thinking about small shifts to routines and environments. The book supplies a completed worksheet as a reference example and insists there are no right or wrong answers.

Sources:
- "During your pause and reflect, complete the Generalization Checklist below."
- "Take 10–15 minutes to observe your home using the Self-Assessment Generalization Checklist provided:"
- "Note: There are no right or wrong answers here. This is about noticing patterns, not fixing anything just yet."

nodes.title: Optional community discussion: where does the skill work, and what would the other setting need?
nodes.description:
The optional weekly discussion, titled "Helping Without Taking Over", asks the parent to name a skill their child uses in one place but not another, then work out what helped in the successful setting and what is missing in the other. A bonus prompt asks them to pick one routine to start applying the Prompting Hierarchy to this week and to decide which support level to start at. The book frames sharing in the private group as optional, with listening in offered as a valid form of participation.

Sources:
- "Where have you already seen your child successfully use a skill in one place, but not yet in another?"
- "Think about one routine where you could begin using the Prompting Hierarchy this week. What support level would you start with?"
- "Join our Community Discussion Thread in the private group to share your reflections, ask questions, or simply listen in."

nodes.title: A recorded baseline and "aha" moments that become the foundation for Lesson 2
nodes.description:
The lesson's own deliverable is not a changed routine but a documented starting point: the completed worksheet plus whatever noticings the parent jots down. The book states these reflections carry forward as the foundation for the next lesson's work on the home setup. It closes by naming what the parent has already done, observing everyday moments and seeing how structure, visuals and simple supports reduce frustration, and hands off to Lesson 2 on the home environment.

Sources:
- "Once you've completed the worksheet, feel free to jot down any “aha” moments that stood out. These reflections will serve as a foundation for Lesson 2, when we begin creating a more communication-friendly setup at home."
- "In the next lesson, we’ll build on this foundation by making small, practical changes to your home environment so communication becomes clearer and easier for everyone."

nodes.title: Set up the home so the child can show what they need and the parent can understand
nodes.description:
Lesson 2's headline goal is environmental, not corrective: the parent reshapes the house so that communication becomes easier on both sides of the exchange. The lesson frames this against the daily experience of guessing what an upset child wants, and contrasts it with a child tapping a picture by the door and being understood immediately. It explicitly disclaims fixing the child or forcing speech, and the changes are meant to be gradual and small. Everything else in the lesson hangs off this goal.

Sources:
- "Not fixing your child. Not forcing words. Not getting everything perfect. It’s about slowly shaping your home environment so communication becomes easier for your child to show you what they need and easier for you to understand them."
- "In this lesson, we’ll start taking small, thoughtful steps to turn your home into a space that naturally supports and encourages communication."
- "Many parents describe this stage as incredibly draining, not because their child is “too much,” but because so much of the day is spent trying to decode what their child is feeling or wanting."

nodes.title: Communication is not automatically obvious or rewarding, so it has to be taught clearly
nodes.description:
The lesson's core teaching premise is that the link between signalling and being understood may not form on its own for a child on the spectrum. Some children attend more to objects, patterns, and routines than to faces, so the ordinary social payoffs of smiles and praise may not motivate repetition. The lesson also notes that everyday interaction stacks language, tone, facial expression, and timing all at once, which takes longer to process. Together these justify direct instruction, repetition, and structured input rather than expecting learning by observation.

Sources:
- "Some children don’t automatically realize that communication can get them something helpful. That connection “When I show you what I want, someone understands me” sometimes needs to be taught clearly and gently."
- "As a result, the usual social rewards, smiles, praise, or facial expressions, may not be motivating on their own."
- "There’s language, tone, facial expressions, and timing all happening at once. For some children, it simply takes a bit longer to process everything."

nodes.title: The "Before" pantry response: hand over the snack to head off a meltdown
nodes.description:
The lesson names the default parental move at the pantry as a concrete approach and then sets it aside. It works in the narrow sense of preventing an escalation, but the lesson's objection is that nothing is learned in the exchange because the child never gets to signal anything. It is presented as the baseline the parent is being asked to change, not as a technique to keep.

Sources:
- "Before: Your child walks over to the pantry and starts to become frustrated. You hand over their usual snack to avoid a meltdown. It’s a quick fix, but there’s no chance to support communication."

nodes.title: The "After" pantry response: picture on the pantry, gentle point, wait, then label and deliver
nodes.description:
The alternative approach puts a picture of the desired item where the child already goes, then inserts a pause and a gentle point before the item is handed over. The child's touch or glance is accepted as the communication, and the parent names it aloud while delivering. The lesson treats this sequence as the seed of the whole method: the child learns the contingency between signalling and getting something good.

Sources:
- "After: You place a picture of a banana on the outside of the pantry. When your child walks over, you pause, point gently to the picture, and wait. Your child touches it or glances at it. You smile and say, “Banana!” then hand it over."
- "Now your child is beginning to understand: When I do this, something good happens. That moment is the beginning of communication."

nodes.title: At the pantry, choose between the quick fix and building a communication opportunity
nodes.description:
The lesson stages an explicit Before/After choice at the same everyday moment, which makes this a genuine decision point rather than a bare recommendation. Both branches end with the child getting the snack; what differs is whether a chance to communicate was created or spent. The book endorses the After version and characterises the Before version as a missed opportunity.

Sources:
- "Let’s walk through a quick example:"
- "It’s a quick fix, but there’s no chance to support communication."
- "That moment is the beginning of communication."

nodes.title: Pause and silently count to five to give the child processing time
nodes.description:
The lesson singles out the pause as the simplest high-yield thing a parent can do, with a concrete implementation: count to five silently before filling the silence. The rationale is processing delay, not defiance or inability, so slowing the pace and breaking things down is framed as removing pressure rather than lowering expectations. This is the action the parent performs inside the After version of the pantry moment and anywhere else a response is expected.

Sources:
- "One of the most effective strategies is also one of the simplest: pause. Giving your child a few extra seconds, perhaps counting to five silently, allows them the time they need to understand and respond."
- "Processing delays are common, and slowing or breaking things down can make communication feel much more manageable and successful."

nodes.title: Alex and Jack: a swing picture by the back door replaced daily screaming
nodes.description:
A father, Alex, described his son Jack screaming when he wanted to go outside, with no one able to tell what he wanted. A visual of the family's backyard swing was added near the back door, and one day Jack ran over and tapped it. Alex reported it as the first time he felt his son had genuinely told him something. The story is the lesson's clearest demonstration that a single placed picture can convert distress into a message.

Sources:
- "One dad I worked with, Alex, told me about how his son Jack would often scream when he wanted to go outside."
- "We added a visual of their backyard swing near the back door. One day, Jack ran over and tapped the picture."
- "Jack had a way to communicate, and Alex had a way to listen."

nodes.title: The child learns communication gets results, and the pattern becomes one they trust
nodes.description:
The predicted result of repeatedly staging these moments is a learned contingency: the child comes to expect that signalling produces a response. The lesson describes this as becoming a pattern the child understands and trusts over time, and says that is the point at which communication starts to grow. It reinforces the claim with the figure that most communication is nonverbal, so gestures and glances count as real progress even without speech.

Sources:
- "By setting up clear, visual cues and routines in your space, your child begins to understand that communication gets results."
- "Over time, this becomes a powerful pattern they understand and trust. And that’s when communication begins to grow."
- "It’s important to remember that over 90% of communication is nonverbal."

nodes.title: A Choice Board of pictured options the child can point to
nodes.description:
The first predictability tool introduced is a board of pictures the child selects from, illustrated with breakfast items such as waffle, banana, or yogurt. Its stated value is that preference can be expressed without the child having to retrieve words. It is the tool the lesson walks through first and the one carried by the Sam and Leo story.

Sources:
- "A Choice Board: For example, a board with pictures of different breakfast items. Your child can point to “waffle,” “banana,” or “yogurt” to indicate their choice. This helps them express preferences without needing to find the words."

nodes.title: A First-Then board near the play area
nodes.description:
A two-slot board placed where play happens makes a sequence of expectation visible, with the lesson's example pairing a clean-up task with an iPad reward. It is offered as one of the simple ways to introduce predictability rather than as a behaviour programme. Like the other tools, its job is to make what comes next legible without requiring the child to hold it in memory.

Sources:
- "A First-Then board near the play area: “First clean up blocks, then iPad.”"
- "Visuals support processing: When the steps of a routine are visible, your child doesn’t have to hold them all in their memory."

nodes.title: A visual schedule on the bedroom door showing the steps of bedtime
nodes.description:
A posted sequence of the evening's steps — bath, pyjamas, story, sleep — is offered as a way to make a routine visible at the point of use. The lesson's justification is that a visible routine frees the child from holding the steps in memory and lets them know what comes next, which it links to comfort and safety. One of the anonymous family examples later shows the same idea applied at the nightstand.

Sources:
- "A visual schedule on the bedroom door: showing bedtime steps, bath, pyjamas, story, sleep."
- "Routines create comfort: When your child knows what comes next, they feel safer, and that sense of security opens the door to connection."

nodes.title: Labels on bins so the child can find and put away their own toys
nodes.description:
Labelling storage is the lowest-effort tool in the set, and its stated purpose is two-directional: finding favourites and knowing where they go back. The lesson groups it with the other supports as a signpost guiding the child toward independence and interaction, and Karen's story later reports meltdown reduction from exactly this change.

Sources:
- "Labels on bins: so your child knows where to find favourite toys or where to put them away."
- "Think of them as little signposts around your home guiding your child gently toward independence and interaction."

nodes.title: Pick which simple support to add first to make the home predictable
nodes.description:
The lesson lays out four named tools and frames them as a menu of ways to begin, so the parent chooses an entry point rather than installing everything. The governing criterion is that predictability means the child knows what to expect, not that the household becomes rigidly scheduled. All four options are endorsed; the distinction the book draws is between a predictable home and a rigid one.

Sources:
- "Here are a few simple ways to introduce predictability:"
- "But predictability doesn’t mean a rigid schedule; it means your child knows what to expect. That clarity builds comfort, and that sense of security opens the door to connection."

nodes.title: Place the chosen visuals and labels where the routine actually happens
nodes.description:
The doing part of the home-setup half of the lesson is physical placement: pictures on the pantry, a board on the kitchen wall, a schedule on the bedroom door, labels on bins, a visual near the back door. The lesson insists the placement is intentional and located at the point of need rather than centralised. It reads the resulting message to the child as one of belonging and trust in the space.

Sources:
- "Each of these tools sends a simple message: You can trust this space. You belong here."
- "Now that you’ve started to see how placing objects and pictures intentionally around your home can support communication"
- "we’ll take this idea one step further and walk through exactly how to begin creating that predictability in your home one small, powerful change at a time."

nodes.title: Sam and Leo: a kitchen-wall Choice Board produced Leo's first unprompted choice
nodes.description:
Sam put a Choice Board of common snacks on the kitchen wall. Her son Leo, who had difficulty with words, pointed clearly at the cracker picture one morning — the first choice he had made without fuss or frustration. Sam characterised it as small in scale but large in emotional weight, which is how the lesson frames the whole set of changes.

Sources:
- "One parent, Sam, placed a Choice Board on the kitchen wall with pictures of common snacks."
- "Her son, Leo, had difficulty using words, but one morning, he pointed clearly to the “cracker” picture. It was the first time he made a choice without fuss or frustration."
- "Sam described it as a tiny victory with a big emotional impact."

nodes.title: Karen: toy bins labelled with words and pictures reduced meltdowns and built independence
nodes.description:
Karen labelled her son's toy bins using both words and pictures rather than one or the other. The reported result accumulated over time rather than appearing at once: fewer daily meltdowns and more independence in both choosing toys and putting them away. It is the lesson's evidence that labelling storage is not merely tidy but communicative.

Sources:
- "One parent, Karen, shared that she labelled her son’s toy bins with both words and pictures. It was a small shift, but over time, it reduced daily meltdowns and helped her son become more independent when choosing or cleaning up toys."

nodes.title: An unnamed family: a bedtime-book visual on the nightstand eased the transition to sleep
nodes.description:
One family placed a picture of their child's favourite bedtime book on the nightstand. The cue let the child anticipate what was coming, and the reported effect was a smoother transition into sleep with fewer protests. The lesson uses it to show that a single visual can do the work of a whole schedule when it marks a familiar routine.

Sources:
- "Another family added a visual of their child’s favourite bedtime book to the nightstand. That small cue helped their child anticipate the routine and eased the transition to sleep with fewer protests."

nodes.title: Raj: a laminated picture of shoes by the front door led to his daughter's first consistent initiations
nodes.description:
Raj laminated a picture of shoes and put it by the front door. His daughter began pointing to it whenever she wanted to go outside, and the lesson flags this specifically as the first time she initiated an activity consistently — which ties the home-setup half of the lesson directly to the initiation half. It is the clearest case in the text of environment producing initiation rather than just smoother responding.

Sources:
- "A dad named Raj placed a laminated picture of shoes by the front door. His daughter began pointing to it each time she wanted to go outside. It was the first time she had initiated an activity consistently."
- "These small changes helped communication blossom in ways families hadn’t expected, and each one started with a simple, intentional support."

nodes.title: Notice whether the child is initiating or responding, without labelling them
nodes.description:
The second half of the lesson shifts from changing the house to observing the child, and sets awareness rather than intervention as the objective. The lesson sorts communication into initiator and responder behaviours and is careful to say the categories are for spotting patterns, not for labelling the child. Creating initiation opportunities is deferred to the next lesson; this lesson stops at looking.

Sources:
- "As you begin making changes in your home, take one more gentle step: begin noticing how your child communicates. This is not about pressure. It’s simply about becoming more aware."
- "When we look closely, most communication fits into two simple categories. Not to label your child, but to help you notice patterns. Initiator behaviours and responder behaviours."
- "Before we create those opportunities next lesson, we’re going to focus on observation."

nodes.title: Initiating is harder than responding because it takes four steps without a reminder
nodes.description:
The lesson decomposes initiation into knowing what you want, realising you can tell someone, deciding how, and then doing it — and notes that it must happen without a prompt from anyone else. It cites research that children on the spectrum need more chances to initiate, and reframes a child who rarely initiates as someone who needs the skill built slowly rather than someone who cannot. This premise is why the lesson asks the parent to count initiator and responder behaviours separately.

Sources:
- "Research shows that children on the spectrum often need more chances to initiate or start communication."
- "Initiating communication is harder than responding. It means your child has to: 1.​ Know what they want 2.​ Realize they can tell someone 3.​ Decide how to tell them 4.​ And then actually do it"
- "So if your child isn’t initiating much yet, that doesn’t mean they can’t; it just means we’ll build it slowly."

nodes.title: The park story: hand-pulling and standing by the swing were the message all along
nodes.description:
A mother contrasted another child at the park who said "Push me higher!" with her own son, who took her hand, pulled her to the swings, and stood beside the empty seat looking back at her. She first read it as aimless wandering, then recognised the hand pull as "come with me" and the standing as "I want to go on." The lesson uses it to show that initiation was already occurring in a non-spoken form, and that recognising it changed how the parent watched.

Sources:
- "Instead, he walked over, grabbed her hand, and pulled her toward the swings. When they got there, he stood beside the empty seat and looked back at her."
- "Pulling her hand was his way of saying, “Come with me.”​ Standing beside the swing meant, “I want to go on.”"
- "She stopped waiting only for words and started noticing the gestures, the looks, the little actions her son used to share what he needed."

nodes.title: Detailed Communication Tracking Sheet: antecedent, communication, response
nodes.description:
The first worksheet records each moment in three columns — what happened before, what the child did, and what happened after — plus date and time. The worked sample logs five moments across one day, from pointing at a milk cup to pushing a plate forward. The lesson says to reach for this sheet when the question is which situations are generating communication opportunities in the first place.

Sources:
- "Shows what happened before, what your child did, and what happened after the communication."
- "Use when you want to understand what situations create communication opportunities."
- "What this log helps you notice: ●​ What situations create communication opportunities ●​ How their child communicates (words, gestures, sounds) ●​ How adults respond"

nodes.title: Per Occurrence Communication Sheet: tally one skill by time block
nodes.description:
The second worksheet narrows to a single named skill and tallies it across time blocks, also recording how the child communicated and whether a prompt was needed. The completed sample tracks "Asking for 'More'" to a total of ten requests, with a parent note that prompts dropped off later in the day. The lesson assigns this sheet to the question of whether a skill is increasing over time.

Sources:
- "Per Occurrence Tracking Sheet ●​ Focuses on frequency and rate."
- "Use when you want to see if a communication skill is increasing over time."
- "Skill Being Observed: Asking for “More”"

nodes.title: Choose which tracking sheet to use, and whether to observe live or on video
nodes.description:
The lesson presents the two sheets in a comparison table keyed to when to use each, which makes this an explicit choice between named alternatives rather than a single prescribed form. A second choice sits alongside it: watch in real time or record five to fifteen minutes to rewatch later, with recording recommended for a parent who is alone and multitasking. Both sheets are endorsed for their respective purposes.

Sources:
- "Tracking Method | What It Helps You Notice | When To Use It"
- "You can either observe in real-time or record a short video (5–15 minutes is perfect). Recording is helpful if you want to rewatch without multitasking."
- "Download and use your Observation Tracking Sheets:"

nodes.title: Run the six-step observation: pick a moment, define, watch, log, calculate rate, reflect
nodes.description:
The parent activity is a structured observation in six steps. The parent picks a moment when the child is alert (mealtime, playtime, a favourite routine, a quiet puzzle or book), decides in advance what counts as an instance and what does not, watches without announcing it while timing the session, logs each initiator and responder behaviour on the sheet, divides behaviours by minutes to get a rate, and then answers the step-six reflection questions. The lesson's worked arithmetic is 15 behaviours over 10 minutes giving 1.5 per minute.

Sources:
- "Decide ahead of time, so you’re not guessing in the moment: ●​ What does the behaviour look like? ●​ What counts as one instance? ●​ What won’t be counted? ●​ How will you know when a behaviour starts and ends?"
- "●​ Keep things natural, no need to announce you’re recording ●​ Track how long the observation lasts ●​ Mark each initiator and responder behaviour as you see it"
- "●​ Total behaviours observed ÷ Minutes observed = Behaviours per minute"

nodes.title: The parent gets a non-judgmental snapshot of how often and how the child communicates
nodes.description:
The stated product of the activity is a baseline, not an assessment of the child. The lesson repeatedly defuses the scoring reading — it is not a test, it is a window into current skills — and positions today's numbers as the reference point against which later growth will be visible. Step six turns the snapshot into pattern recognition: whether initiator or responder behaviours dominate, and what surprised the parent.

Sources:
- "This isn’t about scoring your child. It’s just about getting a snapshot of today so you can notice growth later."
- "This isn’t a test, it’s just a window into your child’s current communication skills."
- "●​ Did initiator or responder behaviours show up more often? ●​ Were you surprised by anything? ●​ What patterns did you see?"

nodes.title: Answer the reflection prompts and take them to the community discussion
nodes.description:
The lesson bookends the activity with reflection. The Pause and Reflect section asks for one small moment from the week that revealed the child's communication in a new light, and tells the parent to write it down. The weekly discussion section asks which initiator and responder behaviours were seen and whether anything was surprising, with a solo path for parents not in the group. The lesson also reopens Lesson 1's worksheet, asking which generalization skill stood out and whether the small step identified there was tried.

Sources:
- "What was one small moment this week that helped you see your child’s communication in a new light? Jot it down."
- "What initiator behaviours did you see? These might be moments when your child started an interaction on their own."
- "Last Lesson, you used the Self-Assessment of Generalization Strategies worksheet to think about where your child is already using skills across people, places, and things, and where they may still need a little extra support."

nodes.title: Small home changes make communication clearer and calmer, and awareness itself counts as progress
nodes.description:
The closing claims three changes: the home is clearer and calmer for communication, the parent understands why predictability, visuals, and processing time reduce frustration, and the parent has begun reading their child's initiating and responding style. The lesson repeats that nothing was being fixed — the work was noticing what already happens and laying groundwork. It credits the parent even if only reflection, not a full observation, was completed.

Sources:
- "You learned why predictability, visual supports, and extra processing time can reduce frustration and support connection."
- "This lesson wasn’t about fixing anything. It was about noticing what’s already happening and beginning to build a home where communication can flourish."
- "If you’ve made it this far, whether you completed an observation or just thought more deeply about how your child communicates, take a moment to be proud. That awareness is a huge step."

nodes.title: Use visual supports so the child can see what is happening now and what comes next
nodes.description:
Lesson 3's overarching aim is to move the home away from speech-only communication and toward supports the child can see. The lesson frames visuals as a bridge between the child's world and the parent's, and claims that strengthening that bridge makes communication easier for everyone in the house. Concretely the parent should finish the lesson having introduced at least one visual support at home. The lesson positions this as low-stakes: one small change, not a redesign of family life.

Sources:
- "One of the most powerful tools we can use to support communication is visual supports. Visuals slow things down. They make expectations clearer. They help children see what is happening now and what comes next."
- "In many ways, visuals act like a bridge between your child’s world and yours. When that bridge becomes stronger, communication becomes easier for everyone."
- "You don’t need to change everything at once. Even adding one simple visual support can begin to make communication feel clearer and routines more predictable."

nodes.title: Lesson 3 learning outcomes: actions before words, processing load, clarity through visuals
nodes.description:
The lesson states three key points of discussion that function as its learning outcomes. First, that communication often begins in actions rather than words and that unclear expectations feed frustration. Second, that fast verbal input and shifting routines tax processing and understanding. Third, that visual supports supply the clarity and consistency that make comprehension and communication more effective. These three claims are the argument the rest of the lesson builds strategies on.

Sources:
- "Communication may begin through actions rather than words; unclear expectations can contribute to frustration"
- "Fast-paced verbal input and changing routines can impact processing and understanding"
- "Visual supports provide clarity and consistency, supporting comprehension and more effective communication"

nodes.title: Opening vignette: the shoes transition, told once without visuals and once with a schedule
nodes.description:
The lesson opens with a morning scene the parent is meant to recognize: the child is absorbed in play, the parent calls for shoes, and the request ends in crying, dropping to the floor, or running away. The book reads the meltdown not as defiance but as a transition that arrived without warning from the child's point of view. It then replays the same morning with a wall schedule, where the parent narrates "First breakfast… then shoes… then car" and physically removes the finished picture. The child may still hesitate, but the change is no longer a surprise.

Sources:
- "Suddenly, the room fills with big emotions. Your child cries, drops to the floor, or runs away."
- "They were playing. They were focused. And suddenly the activity stopped. They didn’t see the change coming."
- "But now the change isn’t a surprise. They can see it. They can understand what’s coming next. And most importantly, they can begin to prepare for the transition."

nodes.title: Core premise: spoken words vanish on being said, visuals stay put long enough to be processed
nodes.description:
The teaching premise underneath every strategy in Lesson 3 is permanence. Speech is gone the instant it is spoken, which penalizes a child who needs extra time to process; a picture stays on the fridge or the wall and can be returned to. The lesson extends this with a therapist's saying about out-of-sight items and argues that visuals make the invisible visible. It also separates delayed expressive language from comprehension: a child who cannot say it may still understand, and often understands visually better than verbally.

Sources:
- "Instead of relying only on spoken language, which disappears the moment it’s said, visuals stay in place long enough for children to process, understand, and respond."
- "As therapists often say, “If something is out of sight, it’s likely out of mind”, especially for early learners. Visuals help make the invisible visible."
- "It’s also important to remember that a language delay doesn’t always mean a child doesn’t understand."

nodes.title: Review of the previous lesson: is your child an initiator or a responder?
nodes.description:
Before introducing visuals, the lesson sends the parent back to the tracking work of the previous lesson and asks what pattern it revealed. Initiator behaviours are unprompted: pointing at a snack, seeking help, greeting first. Responder behaviours wait for someone else to open the exchange: following a direction, waving back, answering a question. The lesson insists the point is not a verdict but a starting position, so the parent can meet the child where they actually are.

Sources:
- "Based on your communication tracking sheet, did you notice whether your child tends to initiate interactions or more often responds to others?"
- "Responder-style communicators often wait for someone else to notice their need. They typically don’t seek others out but will respond when prompted."
- "When we understand where our child is in this moment, we can meet them there with compassion, not pressure and take the next step together to gently grow their communication and independence."

nodes.title: The yogurt problem: a wanted item with no way to ask for it ends in mutual frustration
nodes.description:
The lesson uses a short hypothetical to show the cost of having no visual channel. A child wants yogurt, lacks the words, and is left with tantrum, whining, or dragging the parent by the hand to the fridge; the parent is left guessing. The book puts a clock on it: five minutes in, both people are frustrated. This example is the gap that choice boards are introduced to close, and it is paired with the claim that not knowing what the child needs is one of the hardest parts of parenting a child with a language delay.

Sources:
- "Let’s say your child wants yogurt but doesn’t have the language to ask for it. Will they tantrum? Whine? Try to guide you to the fridge by hand? And how do you know what they’re asking for? Five minutes in, both of you might be frustrated."
- "For many parents, one of the most challenging parts of supporting a child with language delays is simply knowing what their child needs or wants."

nodes.title: Cited research: visuals aid processing and decision-making, and pairing them with speech aids comprehension
nodes.description:
The lesson grounds its claims in three citations rather than leaving them as opinion. Macdonald et al. (2018) is offered for the claim that visuals give consistent cues supporting processing and decision-making in children with processing delays. Meaden et al. (2011) supports pairing visuals with spoken language to raise comprehension. May (2019) is attached specifically to choice boards, and Arthur-Kelly et al. (2009) to left-to-right sequencing. The research is used to justify the lesson's choice of tools.

Sources:
- "Research backs this up: Visual supports are essential for children with processing delays or language challenges. They provide consistent cues that support information processing and decision-making (Macdonald et al., 2018)."
