The book defines the IAS as a picture, word or object to-do list that guides the child through a sequence without adult reminders, and distinguishes it from the Lesson 6 visual schedule: a visual schedule answers what is coming next and is adult-led, while an IAS answers how the child finishes by themselves. Structurally it is always three things — a format (binder, folder, tablet), tasks with a definite beginning and end, and a reward placed at the end of the sequence. That three-part anatomy is the premise every strategy in the lesson instantiates.

Sources:
- "personalized "to-do list" for your child. Using pictures, words, or objects, it guides them through a sequence of activities without needing constant adult reminders."
- "It answers: “What do I do, and how do I finish it by myself?”"
- "The Reinforcer: A "reward" activity or item placed at the very end of the sequence to motivate completion."

nodes.title: First-Then board — the two-step entry point and bridge into IAS
nodes.description:
The simplest IAS format is a high-contrast two-column board: one non-preferred task on the left, one highly motivating activity on the right. The book positions it for children who struggle with transitions or get overwhelmed by a long list, and explicitly calls it a bridge for those not yet ready for a multi-step binder. It is the same tool introduced in Lesson 6, now repurposed as the lowest rung of the independence ladder.

Sources:
- "This is a high-contrast, two-step visual. It is designed to communicate a simple expectation: "Complete the non-preferred task first, then get the reward.""
- "Best For: Individuals who struggle with transitions or become overwhelmed by a long list of instructions."
- "A First-Then board is the simplest form of an Independent Activity Schedule, often used as a "bridge" for those who aren't yet ready for a multi-step binder."

nodes.title: Bin System — one activity per labelled bin, arranged in completion order
nodes.description:
Each task lives in its own bin, tray or folder; each bin carries a picture or word label matching the schedule; the bins are lined up in the order the child will work through them. The book credits this arrangement with cutting confusion, raising on-task behaviour and building independence, and it is the only strategy in the lesson given a research citation. This is the format the parent activity and the step-by-step setup both assume.

Sources:
- "Each task is placed in a separate bin, tray, or folder."
- "Bins are arranged in the order your child will complete them."
- "Research Spotlight: Structured teaching strategies like the Bin System are evidence-based practices that increase independence and reduce problem behaviours in children with autism (Howley, 2015)."

nodes.title: Multi-step activity binder — a 3–5 icon Velcro strip for longer independent stretches
nodes.description:
The most advanced format is a binder or vertical strip: a Velcro page holding clear photos or symbols for three to five tasks, paired with numbered workstation bins and a large Finished box at the end of the workspace. The book's worked example runs block tower, then colouring page, then snack as the reward. It is presented as the step you take after the reward contingency is already understood, and its purpose is stamina rather than novelty.

Sources:
- "Once the concept of "doing a task to get a reward" is mastered, you can transition to a binder or a vertical strip. This builds stamina and longer periods of independent play or work."
- "The Icons: Use clear photos or symbols for 3–5 tasks."
- "The "Finished" Box: A large bin at the end of the workspace where all completed tasks are placed."

nodes.title: Choose the IAS format that matches where the child is: First-Then, bins, or a multi-step binder
nodes.description:
The lesson lays the three formats side by side and tells the parent to select by readiness, not ambition — the First-Then board when a list would overwhelm, the bin system to structure a short sequence, the binder only once the task-for-reward idea is mastered. The governing rule is explicit: pace before complexity. This is a staged choice rather than a permanent one, since each format is described as a step toward the next.

Sources:
- "Always move at your child's pace, confidence first, complexity later!"
- "A multi-step activity binder is more complex and helps your child build independence by visually guiding them through a sequence of tasks, increasing focus, stamina, and confidence."
- "A bin system organizes tasks into clear, structured steps, helping your child understand what to do, stay focused, and complete activities more independently."

nodes.title: Fill the schedule with already-mastered tasks: closed-ended, functional, or leisure
nodes.description:
The book's recommended task pool is things the child already knows how to do, sorted into three families: closed-ended activities like puzzles and shape sorters, functional skills like setting the table or folding towels, and creative or leisure items like drawing or looking at a book for five minutes. What every item shares is a definite beginning and end, so the child can tell when it is finished. Familiarity is the point — it leaves the child's attention free for the schedule itself.

Sources:
- "When starting an IAS, it is best to use mastered tasks, things the person already knows how to do."
- "Closed-Ended Tasks: Puzzles, shape sorters, or matching games."
- "The Tasks: Clear, self-contained activities (like a puzzle, a specific worksheet, or a sorting task) that have a definite beginning and end."

nodes.title: Using the IAS to teach a brand-new skill — the approach the lesson warns against
nodes.description:
The lesson names and sets aside the tempting use of an IAS as a teaching vehicle for unlearned skills. Its stated object is the process of following the schedule, so loading the bins with novel content competes with the very thing being taught. The parent activity repeats the constraint from the other direction, restricting selection to activities the child can already complete independently.

Sources:
- "The goal is to teach the process of following the schedule, not to teach a brand-new skill."
- "Step 1: Choose Activities: Select 2 or 3 activities that your child can complete independently (think puzzles, stacking toys, closed ended activities, looking at a favourite book)"

nodes.title: Decide what goes in the bins: known activities, not new learning
nodes.description:
Faced with a choice between rehearsing mastered content and using the schedule to push new skills, the book chooses mastered content outright. The reasoning is that the schedule-following behaviour is the skill under construction, and everything else should be automatic. The reward at the end of the sequence carries the motivation instead.

Sources:
- "When starting an IAS, it is best to use mastered tasks, things the person already knows how to do. The goal is to teach the process of following the schedule, not to teach a brand-new skill."
- "Step 9. Celebrate & Reward: When the child has finished, have them engage in a preferred activity to build motivation around the IAS!"

nodes.title: Level 1 — matching colours or identical pictures
nodes.description:
The introductory rung of the leveled approach pairs identical colours or simple images between the schedule and the bin. The book treats this as foundational discrimination work rather than a task in its own right. A printable Level 1 template is supplied for it.

Sources:
- "At this introductory level, activities focus on basic matching tasks, such as pairing identical colours or simple images. This foundational stage helps children develop essential discrimination skills."
- "Level 1 Template: Matching Colors or Identical Pictures"

nodes.title: Level 2 — matching numbers and related images
nodes.description:
The second rung moves from identity matching to numbers and to associations between different-but-related items, the book's example being a fork matched to a plate. It is framed as cognitive progress: the child is now reasoning about relationships rather than sameness. A Level 2 template accompanies it.

Sources:
- "As children progress, tasks become more complex, involving matching numbers or associating related images (e.g., matching a fork to a plate). This level encourages cognitive development and understanding of relationships between items."
- "Level 2 Template: Matching Numbers"

nodes.title: Level 3 — written word schedules
nodes.description:
The top rung replaces pictures with text, so the child reads and follows written instructions. The book ties this to two payoffs at once — literacy practice and a greater degree of independence and responsibility — and gates it on readiness rather than age. A Level 3 written-word template is provided.

Sources:
- "For children ready to advance further, written schedules are introduced. These schedules require reading and following textual instructions, promoting literacy skills and greater independence."
- "For children ready for more independence, using words instead of pictures promotes literacy skills and responsibility."
- "Level 3: Match Written Words"

nodes.title: Pick the child's level before cutting anything out — confidence first, complexity later
nodes.description:
The leveled approach exists so the parent individualizes rather than defaults, and the setup steps make the choice a concrete gate: you select a level, then cut the matching shapes, numbers or words from that template. The book's tie-breaker is always the child's current pace. Every child's route is treated as unique, so the level is a starting point rather than a ranking.

Sources:
- "Every child’s journey is unique. To meet your child where they are, we can use a leveled approach:"
- "Step 4. Match Visuals: Once you’ve selected your child’s level, cut out the identical shapes, numbers or words. Place one picture on their visual schedule and the other on the bin."
- "Always move at your child's pace, confidence first, complexity later!"

nodes.title: Print, cut and assemble the leveled IAS templates and the All Done pocket
nodes.description:
The lesson's worksheets are an IAS base template plus three leveled sets. The parent prints and cuts the one matching their child's level, puts one copy of each visual on the schedule and its twin on the corresponding bin. The templates also supply the all done pocket and the coloured markers — red circle, yellow star, green triangle — that the routine steps refer to by name.

Sources:
- "Step 3. Step 3: Create the Schedule: Using our IAS templates below, print, cut and make the visual schedule most appropriate for your child."
- "IAS BaseTemplate:"
- "Step 8. Repeat the Sequence: Follow the same sequence for the other two activities (yellow star) and (green triangle)."

nodes.title: Run the nine-step bin setup and the check-do-finish-repeat routine
nodes.description:
The lesson gives a nine-step build: choose two or three independent activities, put one in each of two or three identical bins, make the schedule from the templates, match visuals to bins, arrange the bins in order, guide the routine, move the finished picture to the all done pocket, repeat for the remaining bins, and end on a preferred activity. Running it exercises the same four-beat loop the book describes generally — check the schedule, do the task, signal completion by putting materials away and returning, then move to the next icon. The parent guides while letting the child own the parts they can do alone.

Sources:
- "Step 7. “All Done”: When the activity is completed, redirect the child to the visual schedule and remove the first picture (red circle) and place it in the “all done” pocket"
- "Signal Completion: They put the finished materials away (often in an "All Done" bin) and return to the schedule."
- "Step 6. Guide the Routine: Guide your child through each activity, allowing them to complete parts of the routine independently (like completing the actual activity)"

nodes.title: Parent activity: build a first IAS from 2–3 enjoyed activities and practice it daily
nodes.description:
The week's task is concrete and small: pick two or three activities the child enjoys, put each in a bin, tray or folder, make a visual schedule from pictures, numbers or words, and walk the child through it at least once a day. The book adds a tone instruction — keep each session short and stop on a success, because ending well is what brings the child back tomorrow. The leveled templates are the supplied materials for this build.

Sources:
- "Choose 2–3 simple activities your child enjoys."
- "Practice guiding your child through the schedule at least once per day."
- "Keep sessions short and positive. Ending on a successful note will keep your child motivated to try again tomorrow!"

nodes.title: Reflection: name what independence looks like for this child right now
nodes.description:
Before building anything, the parent is asked to sit with four questions — which small tasks the child could already do with support, where they are already trying, how a bin or visual might extend that, and what independence actually means for this child today. The last prompt asks how the parent will mark small wins daily. The framing is explicitly anti-leap: meaningful steps accumulate into confidence.

Sources:
- "Take a deep breath and reflect: What small tasks could my child do independently with the right support? Have I noticed moments where they’re already trying?"
- "What does independence look like for my child right now?"
- "Remember, it’s not about big leaps, it’s small, meaningful steps that build confidence over time."

nodes.title: Karla: two bins, sitting alongside at first, unprompted completion within two weeks
nodes.description:
Karla began with the minimum viable IAS — one bin for a block tower, one for a picture book — and initially sat beside her son through the whole schedule. The fading happened fast: inside two weeks he worked through both activities with no prompting from her. The story is the lesson's demonstration that a two-bin start is enough and that parent proximity is meant to be temporary.

Sources:
- "Karla started with just two bins: building a tower with blocks and flipping through a picture book. At first, she sat beside her son during the entire schedule. Within two weeks, he was completing both activities without her prompting!"

nodes.title: Alex: IAS applied to a self-care routine — teeth, shoes, backpack — now done solo
nodes.description:
Alex put the IAS on the morning routine rather than on tabletop work: brush teeth, then shoes, then backpack ready. He started with full adult support and now finishes the whole sequence alone, with pride attached to it. The vignette evidences the lesson's claim that the tool stretches beyond work tasks into self-care and chores.

Sources:
- "Alex used a simple IAS for morning routines: brush teeth → put on shoes → backpack ready. He started with full adult support, but now proudly finishes his morning routine solo!"
- "Flexibility: While often used for academic or "work" tasks, IAS can be applied to self-care routines (getting dressed), chores, or even structured leisure time."

nodes.title: Jamal: stocking the bins with LEGOs and sensory bins turned independent work into something requested
nodes.description:
Jamal chose familiar, preferred materials for his daughter's schedule, and the effect was on motivation rather than compliance — she came to love her independent work time and now asks for her special bins each morning. The story backs the parent activity's instruction to choose activities the child enjoys, and shows the reinforcement logic working before the reward is even reached.

Sources:
- "Jamal found that using familiar and preferred activities (like LEGOs and sensory bins) helped his daughter love her independent work time. Now, she asks for her “special bins” every morning!"

nodes.title: Prompt dependency drops as the instruction moves from the parent's voice to the visual
nodes.description:
The lesson's headline result is a transfer of control: the cue to act comes from the schedule instead of from an adult, so the child stops waiting to be told what to do next. Alongside it the book claims executive-function practice — planning, organizing, staying on task — and reduced anxiety from knowing what is coming. The whole design of the routine, ending with the child returning to the schedule rather than to the parent, is what produces this.

Sources:
- "Reduces Prompt Dependency: It shifts the "instruction" from a person's voice to a visual cue, which helps prevent the individual from waiting for someone to tell them what to do next."
- "Builds Executive Functioning: It practices planning, organizing, and staying on task."
- "Predictability: Knowing exactly what is coming next reduces anxiety and helps manage transitions between different types of activities."

nodes.title: Confidence, less frustration, and a caregiver who can step back
nodes.description:
The book predicts four connected changes: the child gains confidence from evidence they can finish things alone, frustration falls because the steps are clear and predictable, flexibility grows through varied tasks, and the caregiver is freed to step back while still being present. The closing frames the week's work as the child learning to start, follow through and finish with less support. The lesson's stated formula for getting there is structure combined with individualization.

Sources:
- "Builds confidence by showing your child they can complete tasks independently."
- "Frees up caregivers to step back while still providing support."
- "The key takeaway: Structure + Individualization = Greater Independence and Success"

nodes.title: Help the child navigate change and new experiences by making the unknown predictable
nodes.description:
Lesson 8 states four learning outcomes for the parent: prepare the child for change, use social stories, introduce a star marker inside familiar routines, and leave the child calmer and more prepared. It frames the lesson as the next step after Lesson 7's independence work, moving from "what do I do now" to "what is coming next." The whole unit is organised around one question posed in the opening vignette: what if the child could see it coming?

Sources:
- "Prepare your child for changes and new experiences"
- "Use social stories to make the unknown feel predictable"
- "Help your child feel calmer, more confident, and more prepared"

nodes.title: Premise: change is hard because the child cannot see it coming, not because they cannot cope
nodes.description:
The lesson opens with a parent announcing a dentist visit and the child shutting down, and reframes that reaction as a information problem rather than a behaviour problem. For children who rely on routine, the unknown is overwhelming and sudden change feels unsafe. The teaching that follows rests on this premise: children often struggle because they do not understand what will happen or what is expected, not because the situation is beyond them.

Sources:
- "But from their perspective… it came out of nowhere."
- "The unknown can feel overwhelming"
- "Sudden changes can feel unsafe"

nodes.title: Social stories: make the parent's plan visible to the child before the event
nodes.description:
The first approach the lesson offers is the social story, a short structured account of an upcoming situation that answers who, what, where, when, why and how. Its function is to move information out of the parent's head and into a form the child can see, so the child is brought into the plan rather than expected to follow along. The lesson lists dentist, doctor, haircut, visitors, starting school, transitions and outings as situations it suits.

Sources:
- "Simply put, Social Stories take what’s happening inside your mind (your plan, your expectations, your understanding of the situation) and make it visible and clear for your child."
- "A social story typically answers key questions like who, what, where, when, why, and how."

nodes.title: The star system: a neutral visual marker that signals "today is a little different"
nodes.description:
The second approach is a star placed into a schedule the child already knows, standing for a small, flexible, non-threatening difference. It is presented as a way to make change itself visible rather than to explain any one event, and the lesson pairs it with a social story so the child both sees that change is coming and understands what the change is. It is explicitly for children already comfortable with a visual schedule or IAS.

Sources:
- "By adding a star into a familiar routine, you’re gently showing that something will be a little different, without it feeling overwhelming."
- "The star represents something slightly different, a small change, a flexible moment."
- "Paired with a Social Story the change will feel less overwhelming."

nodes.title: Explaining or pushing through during the stressful moment itself
nodes.description:
The lesson names, and sets aside, the default approach of handling the situation as it happens: explaining in the car, insisting through the appointment, teaching while the child is already dysregulated. It argues a calm child can take in information and rehearse, while a stressed one cannot, and it tells parents not to read the story during stress or on the way out the door. Poppy's family is the worked example of abandoning this route.

Sources:
- "They also work because they support learning before the situation happens, rather than trying to teach during a stressful moment."
- "Choose a calm moment: not during stress or right before rushing out the door"

nodes.title: Prepare before the event rather than manage it in the moment
nodes.description:
Faced with the three routes, the lesson commits to front-loading: the story is read while the child is calm, days ahead, and the star goes on the schedule before the day arrives. It explicitly rejects doing the teaching inside the stressful moment. It also settles the aim of the whole approach, which is not to shield the child from change but to equip them to handle it.

Sources:
- "Review the social story when your child is calm, not in the middle of the stressful moment."
- "The goal is not to avoid change. It’s to teach your child how to handle it."

nodes.title: Pick one situation and break it into who, what, where, when, why and how
nodes.description:
Steps 1 and 2 of the build process: choose a single routine, event or challenge the child needs help understanding, then decompose it into the six questions the child may not be able to ask. The lesson treats this decomposition as the engine of the whole tool, turning one large uncertain experience into a short predictable sequence. Its own examples of situations to pick are the dentist, a haircut, a visitor, or starting school.

Sources:
- "Pick one routine, event, or challenge your child may need help understanding, like going to the dentist, getting a haircut, having a visitor, or starting school."
- "A social story answers: Who, What, Where, When, Why, and How"

nodes.title: Write it in short reassuring sentences, add matching visuals, and name what the child can do
nodes.description:
Steps 3 to 5 govern how the story is written: short calm sentences without excess detail, optional photos, pictures, symbols or drawings aligned to each step, and concrete coping actions the child can take. The lesson's own coping examples are holding a parent's hand, taking a deep breath, sitting in the chair, and asking for help. It also gives a compact template for the arc: what is happening, what I might see or hear, what I can do, why it is okay.

Sources:
- "Use short, clear sentences your child can understand. Aim for calm, positive language that explains what to expect without adding too much detail."
- "You can use real photos, simple pictures, symbols, or drawings to match each step."
- "Include simple coping or action steps, such as:"

nodes.title: Choose the story format that matches the child's age and learning style
nodes.description:
The lesson asks the parent to make an explicit format choice rather than defaulting to one presentation. It lists picture based, text based, colouring, video, comic book and photo stories, and says the right one depends on the child's age, learning style and the situation being prepared for. The stated deciding criterion is connection: a child who engages with the story learns from it.

Sources:
- "Social stories can look very different depending on a child’s age, learning style, and the situation you’re preparing for."
- "No matter the format, the key is choosing a version that feels accessible, engaging, and meaningful for your child, because when a child connects with the story, they’re much more likely to learn from it."

nodes.title: Picture or photo based story for younger children
nodes.description:
The format the lesson names as usually most effective for younger children, built from real photos, simple illustrations or symbols showing each step in order. Using familiar people, places and objects is said to make the story feel more meaningful and easier to grasp. This is the format that pairs most directly with the visual supports built in earlier lessons.

Sources:
- "For younger children, visual or picture-based social stories are often the most effective."
- "These use real photos, simple illustrations, or symbols to show what will happen step by step."

nodes.title: Text based story for children who have outgrown pictures
nodes.description:
As children grow, the lesson allows the story to carry more detail and rely on written language rather than images. It is listed among the six named formats and presented as a developmental step rather than a different tool. The six questions and the reassuring tone stay the same; only the presentation shifts.

Sources:
- "As children grow, stories can become more detailed, sometimes shifting to text-based formats that rely more on written language and less on visuals."
- "Text based social story"

nodes.title: Interactive formats: colouring booklets, video stories, and comic strips with speech bubbles
nodes.description:
The lesson groups three more participatory formats. Colouring booklets let the child work through the routine page by page; digital stories, tablet versions and video modelling add movement, sound and repetition for children drawn to screens; comic strips use speech bubbles to show what people say or think, which the lesson recommends for social interactions such as turn taking, asking for help, or reading another person's perspective. A comic strip template is supplied with the lesson's worksheets.

Sources:
- "Coloring books or booklets allow children to engage with the story by coloring each page as they learn the routine or skill."
- "Similarly, digital stories or videos, such as PowerPoint presentations, tablet-based stories, or video modelling, can bring the story to life through movement, sound, and repetition"
- "Another engaging format is the use of comic strip-style social stories."

nodes.title: Worked example: the "Going to the Dentist" story mapped to the six questions
nodes.description:
The lesson prints a full five-part dentist story and then labels each line with the question it answers, demonstrating the decomposition in practice. The story includes what the child will see (a small mirror and a light), what they can do (sit, open their mouth, hold Mom's hand), and why it is okay (healthy teeth, feeling proud afterwards). It functions as the model parents copy in the parent activity.

Sources:
- "After breakfast, I am going to the dentist with Mom."
- "I can sit in the chair."
- "How: “I can sit, open my mouth, and hold Mom’s hand.”"

nodes.title: Start small: drop a star into a routine the child already knows, and give it a positive meaning
nodes.description:
Steps 1 and 2 of the star system. The star goes first into an existing Independent Activity Schedule for something well practised, such as setting the table, where the change is trivial (a napkin from a different drawer). The parent then narrates it warmly so the symbol is established as positive and neutral rather than a warning, before it is ever used for anything larger.

Sources:
- "Add a star into a routine your child already knows well"
- "Keep the change small and predictable"
- "You might say: “Oh look! A star today. Something different or special is happening.”"

nodes.title: Move the star onto the daily schedule and show what the change actually is
nodes.description:
Step 3 scales the symbol up once its meaning is established: the star moves to the daily visual schedule and sits beside a picture or word naming the specific difference, such as dentist, haircut, Grandma visiting, park, or ice cream after school. The lesson pairs the marker with the content so the child both anticipates change and knows its shape. Its stated purpose is to let the child expect the change, understand it, and stay regulated through it.

Sources:
- "Once you’ve established what the star means (change) now you can add it to your daily visual schedule to represent bigger changes."
- "Pair the star with what’s different (e.g., park, visitor, new step)"

nodes.title: Read the story once a day for a few days before the event, in a calm moment
nodes.description:
Step 4 of the star sequence and steps 6 and 7 of the story build: rehearsal ahead of time, in a relaxed moment, with a positive tone, repeated until the story feels familiar. The lesson says to pair the reading with the star on the schedule and to invite whatever engagement the child offers, pointing or looking included. The story can be adjusted over time as the child's understanding changes.

Sources:
- "Read it together once a day for a few days leading up to the event if possible."
- "Keep your tone positive and reassuring: this is about building comfort, not pressure"
- "Repetition helps your child feel more familiar and confident."

nodes.title: Poppy's family: haircuts that always ended in tears
nodes.description:
The lesson's one family vignette. Poppy's family found every salon visit ended in tears, and rather than forcing the appointment they wrote a four-line social story covering the salon, the chair going up and down, the snip of the scissors, and a sticker at the end. They read it daily for several days beforehand and put a star on the visual schedule on haircut day, using both tools together exactly as the lesson describes.

Sources:
- "Poppy’s family struggled with haircuts. Every visit ended in tears."
- "Instead of trying to push through, they created a simple social story:"
- "“The scissors make a snip sound.”"

nodes.title: Poppy: still nervous, but no meltdown and more cooperation
nodes.description:
The lesson reports a partial rather than total result and presents that honestly as the win. The nervousness remained, but the meltdown did not happen and cooperation improved. This calibrates parent expectations: the tool reduces the intensity of hard moments rather than erasing them.

Sources:
- "The result? Still a little nervous, but no meltdown."
- "More cooperation. A big step forward."

nodes.title: Pause and reflect: where change hits hardest, and what could be prepared in advance
nodes.description:
The reflection section asks the parent to locate the specific moments where change is hardest for their child, to spot what currently arrives unexpectedly, and to pick one small thing they could prepare for ahead of time. It closes with the lesson's central question, echoing the opening vignette. The answers feed directly into choosing the one situation for the week's activity.

Sources:
- "When does my child struggle most with change?"
- "What is something small I could prepare them for in advance?"
- "And most importantly: What might shift if my child could “see it coming”?"

nodes.title: Try it this week: write one social story and put a star on the schedule for that day
nodes.description:
The week's task is a six-step run through the whole method on a single situation: choose it, write it using who/what/where/when/why/how, keep it short and positive, add visuals if useful, read it once a day beforehand, and place a star on the visual schedule on the day itself. It is deliberately scoped to one story rather than a system. The optional extension pack offers fill-in-the-blank templates, change-marker visuals and step-by-step desensitization plans for families needing more repetition or gradual exposure.

Sources:
- "This week, try creating one simple social story using the steps and template provided."
- "Step 5: Read the story with your child​ Once per day before the event"

nodes.title: Worksheets: story outline template, comic strip template, and a completed example
nodes.description:
Three printable supports accompany the activity: a blank story outline, a comic strip template for the speech-bubble format, and a filled-in example showing what a finished story looks like. The completed example matters because it gives parents a reference standard, not just an empty form. These are the concrete materials the parent activity depends on.

Sources:
- "*See below for a Social Story Templates: Story outline and comic book template."
- "Social Story Comic Strip Template:"
- "Completed Social Story Template Example:"

nodes.title: Lower anxiety in the moment, and over time a child who expects and handles change
nodes.description:
The lesson claims two layers of result. Immediately, reduced uncertainty lowers anxiety and produces more regulated, cooperative behaviour during the event itself. Cumulatively, repeated preparation desensitizes the child so new experiences are approached with flexibility and confidence, and change becomes something understood rather than survived. The lesson sums the felt result up in the child's own imagined words.

Sources:
- "This lowers anxiety and helps the child feel more in control, which often leads to more regulated and cooperative behaviour in the moment."
- "Over time, your child learns that change is something they can understand, expect, and handle with confidence."
- "They help your child feel like: “I know what’s coming. I can do this.”"

nodes.title: Leave the course holding one connected system of support rather than eight separate tricks
nodes.description:
The closing unit reframes the whole course: its aim was never to hand the parent a favourite strategy but to assemble a system whose parts reinforce each other. The overview explicitly steps back to show the bigger picture and to let the parent see the accumulated toolkit as a single thing they now own. This is the top goal of the unit, and everything else in the closing hangs off it. It also renames the result as a framework for understanding, not just a set of materials.

Sources:
- "This course was never about one strategy. It was about building a system of support that works together."
- "Throughout this course, you’ve built a toolkit to support your child’s communication, independence, and confidence at home:"
- "What you’ve created is not just a set of tools. It’s a framework for understanding. And importantly, this framework is flexible."

nodes.title: Premise restated: children participate and regulate when their world is made to make sense
nodes.description:
The overview restates the founding premise that justifies every lesson: comprehension comes first. Clear expectations, predictable routines and visually supported communication are named as the conditions, and four capacities are named as what they unlock. This is the principle that makes a system of supports coherent rather than arbitrary. It is stated as a general claim about children, not about one child.

Sources:
- "Children do best when their world makes sense to them."
- "When expectations are clear, when routines are predictable, and when communication is supported visually, not just verbally, children are more able to:"
- "Participate"

nodes.title: The course is reassembled as seven layered domains, from environment through to flexibility
nodes.description:
The overview inventories what was layered over the eight lessons as seven named domains, each with a one-line function. The list is the book's own table of contents rewritten as a set of capabilities rather than topics. Notably prompting is framed as support that stops short of takeover, and independence as incremental. This inventory is how the closing proves to the parent that a system, not a grab-bag, was built.

Sources:
- "Environment → Making things visible, clear, and accessible"
- "Prompting → Supporting without taking over"
- "Flexibility → Preparing for change in a supportive way"

nodes.title: Each tool is shown propping up a different domain, so the parts interlock
nodes.description:
Having listed the domains, the overview pairs each concrete tool with the domain it serves, demonstrating interlock rather than asserting it. A visual schedule is tied to transitions, a choice board to communication, an organised space to independence, and the Social Story from the final lesson to flexibility. The mapping is the mechanical argument behind the claim that the pieces connect. It also functions as a compact index back into the individual lessons.

Sources:
- "Each piece connects."
- "A visual schedule supports a transition."
- "A Social Story supports flexibility."

nodes.title: Keep running every strategy at once and try to do them perfectly
nodes.description:
The closing names, in order to set aside, the approach of maintaining the full toolkit simultaneously and flawlessly. It is raised as the natural temptation at the end of a course that has introduced many tools, and the reflection week is explicitly designed against it. The book's phrasing treats completeness and perfection as the two failure modes to avoid. It is not condemned harshly, only displaced by a smaller commitment.

Sources:
- "What matters most is not doing everything at once, or doing it perfectly, but choosing what works, staying consistent, and allowing those small changes to build over time."
- "This week is about reflection. Keep it simple. You don’t need to do everything, just keep going."

nodes.title: Pick one or two strategies that worked and run them every day
nodes.description:
The alternative the book lays out is deliberately narrow: select the one or two supports that proved most helpful for this child and keep them in daily use. It supplies the shortlist to choose from, all tools drawn from earlier lessons, so the choice is concrete rather than abstract. Consistency over breadth is the operating rule. The payoff is framed as gradual accumulation rather than immediate change.

Sources:
- "Choose one or two strategies that felt most helpful and continue using them daily:"
- "A First-Then board"
- "A Social Story for an upcoming event"

nodes.title: Choose what to keep doing: a sustainable one or two over the whole toolkit
nodes.description:
The overview puts an explicit choice to the parent and answers it in the same sentence — choose what works and stay consistent, rather than attempt everything. The decision converts an eight-lesson curriculum into a maintenance plan the parent can actually sustain after the course ends. It is the hinge of the closing unit: the reflection activities exist to inform it. The book endorses the narrow option and sets aside the exhaustive one.

Sources:
- "What matters most is not doing everything at once, or doing it perfectly, but choosing what works, staying consistent, and allowing those small changes to build over time."
- "Note one strategy you’d like to keep using daily"
- "Choose one area you’d like to continue building"

nodes.title: Run a reflection week: answer the review questions and write down what improved
nodes.description:
Instead of a new technique, the final week's work is structured reflection. The parent sits with four questions about what has changed, which strategies helped, what small wins appeared and what is still unanswered, then commits the answers to paper as two or three improvements, one strategy to keep daily and one area to keep building. Writing it down is what turns the reflection into the maintenance decision. The book keeps the task deliberately small.

Sources:
- "What feels different now compared to when you started?"
- "What small wins have you noticed along the way?"
- "Write down 2–3 things that have improved"

nodes.title: Other families report the same ending: mornings calmer, not perfect
nodes.description:
The examples section reports a shared refrain from parents at this stage — comprehension of the child has grown even though life has not become easy. One family's mornings, previously the worst part of the day, are described as calmer and more predictable under a simple visual schedule and clearer expectations. The book uses the vignette to define what progress is allowed to look like, explicitly disclaiming perfection. It calibrates the parent's expectations at exactly the moment they take stock.

Sources:
- "Many families say the same thing at this stage:“It’s not that everything is suddenly easy…but I understand my child so much more now.”"
- "One parent shared that mornings were once the hardest part of their day."
- "things aren’t perfect, but they’re calmer, smoother, and more predictable. That’s what progress often looks like."

nodes.title: Understanding deepens and small wins accumulate, even where life is still hard
nodes.description:
The result the book claims for the parent who reaches the end is comprehension rather than ease. Progress is characterised as gradual but cumulative, and the evidence is located in ordinary moments — a routine understood, a choice made, a step done alone, a change handled a little better. The book counts each of these as proof that the system is working. It names confidence and connection, not just skills, as what has been built.

Sources:
- "Progress may feel gradual, but it is powerful."
- "Every time your child understands a routine, makes a choice, completes a step independently, or navigates a change with a little more ease, you are seeing the impact of what you’ve created."
- "You are not just supporting skills; you are building confidence, connection, and a foundation your child can carry forward."

nodes.title: Parent shifts from reacting to anticipating, with a framework left over for new problems
nodes.description:
The closing promise has two halves. The parent is described as having moved from in-the-moment reaction to proactive structuring — anticipating needs, arranging the environment, engineering communication opportunities, building independence in systematic steps — while the child is described as gaining functional communication, understanding of expectations and independent participation across routines. The book then concedes that hard moments will keep coming and argues the durable gain is the decision-making framework itself. That framework is what makes the ending a handoff rather than a stopping point.

Sources:
- "You may notice you’re moving from reacting in the moment to taking a more proactive approach, anticipating needs, structuring the environment to increase clarity and success, creating intentional opportunities for communication, and building independence through small, systematic steps."
- "At the same time, your child is developing key foundational skills, understanding expectations, using communication more functionally, and increasing their ability to engage, regulate, and participate more independently across routines."
- "There will still be challenges, and moments that feel less clear. That’s expected. But now you have a framework to guide your decision-making, practical strategies to draw from, and a clearer direction for supporting your child’s ongoing progress and generalization of skills."

nodes.title: Keep going after the last lesson rather than treating the course as finished
nodes.description:
The final section is titled around continuation and offers the parent onward routes instead of an ending. Three are put on the table: an optional extension workbook, an optional community discussion, and a follow-on course. The framing is that the course closes but the work does not, and each route is voluntary. This goal collects the book's onward path.

Sources:
- "7.​ Let’s Keep Going, Together​"
- "You don’t need to do everything, just keep going."
- "Sharing your experience can help others and remind you how far you’ve come."

nodes.title: Optional extension workbook for extra practice and deeper independence work
nodes.description:
The first onward route is a workbook offered as optional, not assigned. It contains further practice ideas, real-life examples, and material aimed at deepening the child's independence and communication — the same two targets the course has pursued throughout. The book positions it as a reference to return to on demand rather than a sequence to complete. That framing keeps it consistent with the decision to do less, consistently.

Sources:
- "If you’d like to continue building on what you’ve learned, the extension workbook offers:"
- "Ways to deepen your child’s independence and communication"
- "Think of it as a guide you can return to whenever you need it."

nodes.title: Optional community discussion to compare takeaways and teach someone else
nodes.description:
The second onward route is a group reflection with other parents, again marked optional. Its prompts ask for the biggest takeaway, changes noticed in the child, sources of pride, remaining questions, and — pointing toward the next course — what the parent could teach a family member. The book argues the exchange benefits both the listener and the speaker. It is the first place the parent is cast as a source of knowledge rather than a recipient.

Sources:
- "6.​ Optional Community Discussion of the Week"
- "What could you teach a family member?"
- "Sharing your experience can help others and remind you how far you’ve come."

nodes.title: Next course: carry the strategies into school, therapy and community as the child's advocate
nodes.description:
The third onward route is a sequel course, previewed twice in this unit. Its subject is generalisation beyond the home — school, community, therapy settings and wider family life — achieved by sharing strategies with others and collaborating to keep them consistent across environments. The stated end point is the parent becoming their child's strongest and most informed advocate. It presumes the home system built by this course is already in place.

Sources:
- "In the next course, you’ll learn how to share this knowledge with your community."
- "Join us in the next course as we explore how to take what you’ve learned here into your child’s school, community, therapy settings, and everyday family life."
- "Most importantly, you’ll continue building the skills to be your child’s strongest and most informed advocate."

nodes.title: Make home a place where the child can communicate and be understood, with less frustration
nodes.description:
This is the single goal the whole course serves and the trunk all eight lessons hang from. The preface states it directly as the promise of the course: simple visual supports used at home, aimed at three linked results — less frustration, more independence, real communication. It is deliberately scoped to the home rather than to therapy or school, and to the parent rather than the professional. The closing overview restates the same goal as a claim about clarity: a world that makes sense is what lets a child participate, communicate, regulate and learn.

Sources:
- "to reduce frustration, support independence, and build meaningful communication."
- "when a home is intentionally set up to support communication"
- "Children do best when their world makes sense to them."

nodes.title: Wait for spoken words and keep explaining, repeating, and adding more language
nodes.description:
The first posture the book weighs and sets aside is the language-first one: treat speech as the measure of communication, and when the child does not respond, say it again, say more, say it louder. The course attacks this on two fronts. Lesson 1 argues most of the message is already being sent non-verbally, so a parent listening only for words misses what is there. Lesson 3 and Lesson 5 add the processing argument — spoken instructions vanish the moment they are said, and extra language overwhelms rather than clarifies.

Sources:
- "Over 90% of communication is non-verbal."
- "While spoken words disappear quickly, visuals"
- "As parents, we often feel the urge to repeat instructions or keep talking in hopes of"

nodes.title: Manage each hard moment as it arrives with a quick fix that heads off the meltdown
nodes.description:
The second rejected posture is reactive management: meet each flashpoint with whatever ends it fastest. Lesson 2 stages this precisely at the pantry — hand over the snack before the frustration escalates — and names the cost: the moment gets survived but no communication is built. The closing overview treats escaping this posture as the course's headline shift for the parent, from managing moments to shaping the surroundings. It is not dismissed as wrong-hearted, only as something that never accumulates.

Sources:
- "hand over their usual snack to avoid a meltdown."
- "Over this course, you’ve moved beyond simply managing moments to thoughtfully"

nodes.title: Make the information visible and the world predictable, and let the child meet it
nodes.description:
The endorsed posture: instead of pressing the child to produce more, change what the child is looking at. The autism primer supplies the justification — these learners often do best with consistent, structured, visual, hands-on support — and the preface frames it as what overwhelmed parents actually asked for, something real and usable today rather than more theory. In practice this means information gets a physical place to live: a picture on the pantry, a board on the fridge, a schedule on the door. The pause after the visual is part of the option, not an afterthought.

Sources:
- "Children with autism often learn best through consistent, structured, visual, and"
- "They need something real. Practical. Something they can use today."
- "you pause, point gently to the picture, and wait"

nodes.title: Change the environment around the child rather than wait for the child to change
nodes.description:
This is the one decision the course is really asking of the parent, and every lesson is downstream of it. Lesson 1 states the form of it — a missing skill at home is a cue problem, not a verdict on the child — and the closing overview names the same move as the arc of the whole course. Choosing it commits the parent to work the child cannot do for them: observing, arranging, printing, placing, and staying consistent. It rules out both waiting for speech and firefighting moment by moment, without calling either of those a moral failure.

Sources:
- "Over this course, you’ve moved beyond simply managing moments to thoughtfully"
- "Children with autism often learn best through consistent, structured, visual, and"
- "Children do best when their world makes sense to them."

nodes.title: Learn to read what the child is already communicating before changing anything
nodes.description:
The first thing the decision commits the parent to is not a change but a look. The preface hands the parent the role by name, Lesson 1 sends them round the house with the Generalization Checklist for ten to fifteen minutes with no change task attached, and Lesson 2 formalises it into a six-step observation that ends in a behaviours-per-minute baseline framed as a snapshot rather than a score. The specific thing being learned to see is non-verbal: hand-pulling, standing by the swing, glancing at a picture. Lesson 2 adds the initiator-versus-responder distinction as the lens for that looking.

Sources:
- "you step into your new role as your child"
- "You’ll learn how to read the non-verbal cues your child is already using"
- "Did initiator or responder behaviours show up more often?"

nodes.title: Give information a physical place to live: put visuals into the rooms where routines happen
nodes.description:
This is the course's central practical commitment and spans Lessons 2 through 4. Lesson 2 places the first supports where the routine actually occurs — choice board, First-Then, schedule, bin labels. Lesson 3 resists the temptation of the full fifteen-item menu and narrows to one board at one moment. Lesson 4 then treats the room itself as part of the visual system: clear containers rather than solid cupboard doors, one room reorganised rather than the whole house, one same-day fix off the Visual Environment Checklist.

Sources:
- "Visuals → Giving information a place to stay"
- "Start with one board (choose a moment in the day)."
- "made your home more predictable and communication-friendly"

nodes.title: Turn the set-up home into a daily rhythm, and match the right support to each moment
nodes.description:
Lessons 5 and 6 convert a furnished home into a working day. Lesson 5 maps the day on the Daily Routine and Transition Planning Chart, sets anchor points and buffer time, and replaces repeated verbal prompting with one direction and a pause. Lesson 6 then adds the selection discipline: a tool that fails usually means the wrong tool, so diagnose whether the child is stuck on choosing or on knowing the steps, and assemble a personalized four-tool toolbox rather than one generic strategy. The reported gain here is modest by design — a smoother transition, fewer prompts.

Sources:
- "build it into a steady rhythm."
- "choosing the right tool for the right moment."
- "calmer response, or your child needing fewer prompts."

nodes.title: Give the support the child needs now, then systematically take it back
nodes.description:
Fading runs the length of the book and is the course's answer to helping without taking over. Lesson 1 introduces the five-level prompting hierarchy used errorlessly — start with strong support, pull back with each success — and Lesson 4 runs a seven-level version ending at independent use of the visual. Lesson 7 completes the move: the Independent Activity Schedule shifts the instruction out of the parent's voice and into the bins, so the child checks, does, finishes and repeats alone. The rule governing it is confidence before complexity, and the bins hold mastered tasks because the skill being taught is schedule-following.

Sources:
- "strong support and slowly pull back over time."
- "Allow your child to use the visual without help."
- "Goal: Child moves from one bin to the next independently."

nodes.title: Make the unknown visible in advance: social stories and a star for days that are different
nodes.description:
The last teaching commitment turns the same logic onto events the routine does not cover. Lesson 8 argues change is hard because the information is hidden, so the parent answers who, what, where, when, why and how before the event, writes it in short reassuring sentences with matching visuals, and reads it once a day in calm moments. A star dropped into a schedule the child already trusts carries the message that today is a little different. The deliberate choice is temporal — prepare beforehand rather than explain mid-meltdown — and the reported result is honest rather than triumphant.

Sources:
- "Make change feel more predictable and less overwhelming"
- "Step 1: Start Small"
- "time to process, prepare, and approach change with greater ease and confidence."

nodes.title: A calmer, more predictable home where the child communicates functionally and participates
nodes.description:
This is the child-side claim the course stakes itself on, and it is stated with unusual restraint. The closing overview reports other families arriving at the same place — mornings not perfect, but calmer and more predictable — and describes the child as using communication more functionally and participating more independently across routines. Individual lessons supply the components: requesting instead of escalating, smoother transitions, unprompted bin completion, a haircut survived without a meltdown. Nothing here is promised as easy.

Sources:
- "engage, regulate, and participate more independently across routines."
- "using communication more functionally"
- "Each piece connects."

nodes.title: A parent who anticipates instead of reacts, holding a framework rather than a pile of tricks
nodes.description:
The parent-side claim is the second half of the book's payoff and the one the closing overview leans on hardest. What the parent ends with is described not as a toolkit but as a framework for understanding, flexible enough to meet problems the course never covered. Sustainability is built into the claim: the instruction is to keep one or two strategies running daily rather than everything at once or perfectly. Lesson 6 marks the earlier waypoint on the same line, where the parent stops guessing and starts choosing on purpose.

Sources:
- "You may notice you’re moving from reacting in the moment to taking a more proactive"
- "now you have a framework to guide your decision-making"
- "What matters most is not doing everything at once, or doing it perfectly, but choosing"

nodes.title: Arc: from adult-led prompting toward the child starting communication unprompted
nodes.description:
In Lesson 1 the parent runs the board, modelling and hand-guiding at the fridge. Lesson 2 names the target explicitly — initiator versus responder — and explains why initiating costs four unprompted steps, then records a baseline; Raj's laminated shoes by the door produce his daughter's first consistent initiations. Lesson 3 asks only that the parent notice whether the child looks and points of their own accord. Lesson 5 makes the parent's own silence the instrument: give the direction once, then wait. Lesson 7 finishes the movement when the instruction leaves the parent's voice entirely, and the closing overview lists both initiating and responding as a domain the course built.

Sources:
- "Initiating communication is harder than responding."
- "Give a direction just once, then pause."
- "Communication → Supporting both initiating and responding"

nodes.title: Arc: from dense errorless prompting to faded support the child no longer needs
nodes.description:
Lesson 1 sets the pattern with a five-level hierarchy run errorlessly — help enough that the child succeeds first time, then step back a level per success, so the prompt fades but the skill remains. Lesson 4 re-runs the same discipline on visuals with a seven-level ladder that terminates in independent use, with Mark's daughter checking her timer unprompted. Lesson 7 states the endpoint as a named problem solved: prompt dependency drops because the schedule, not the adult, now carries the instruction, and Karla's two bins go unprompted within two weeks. The closing overview files the whole arc under one phrase, supporting without taking over.

Sources:
- "the prompt fades, but the skill remains."
- "gradually fade prompts by moving down the"
- "Prompting → Supporting without taking over"

nodes.title: Arc: the widening radius from one snack board to one room to the day to unfamiliar events
nodes.description:
The course expands scope deliberately and refuses to move faster. Lesson 3 permits exactly one board at one moment of the day. Lesson 4 widens to one manageable room, kitchen or playroom, not the house. Lesson 5 takes the whole day, broken into small parts on a planning chart with anchor points and buffer time. Lesson 6 spans routines by matching tools to moments, Lesson 7 covers multi-step sequences the child runs alone, and Lesson 8 reaches events that are not routine at all. Lesson 1's account of generalization is what the widening is for: the skill has to travel across people, places and things.

Sources:
- "Start with one board (choose a moment in the day)."
- "Use this chart to start small and build as you go."
- "Generalization is the ability to take a skill learned in one setting, like therapy or school,"

nodes.title: Arc: from noticing, to measuring, to diagnosing why a support is not working
nodes.description:
The course teaches looking before it teaches doing, and the looking gets sharper each lesson. Lesson 1 assigns observation with no change task attached. Lesson 2 makes it quantitative — a tracking sheet, a six-step protocol, a rate per minute, explicitly a baseline and not a score. Lesson 3 asks only for a week of noticing whether the child looks and points, and Lesson 4 walks the room with a checklist before choosing one fix. By Lesson 6 the same habit has become diagnostic: interrogate why the routine is failing, ask whether the child is stuck on choosing or on the steps. The closing overview ends the course with another round of it.

Sources:
- "Mark each initiator and responder behaviour as you see it"
- "The goal of this lesson was not to create a perfect system, but to start small and notice"
- "choosing the right tool for the right moment."

nodes.title: Arc: from scattered individual tools to one interlocking system of support
nodes.description:
Tools arrive one at a time and are only later shown to interlock. Lesson 2 introduces four placeable supports, Lesson 3 catalogues fifteen types then narrows to one, and Lesson 4 gives each tool its own operating procedure. Lesson 6 is the hinge: supports get deliberately combined — schedule plus video modelling, schedule plus timer, choice board plus emotion cues — under four constraints, and the parent assembles a named toolbox. Lesson 7 adds the IAS, Lesson 8 the social story and star. The closing overview retrospectively renames the pile a system, showing each tool propping up a different domain.

Sources:
- "Instead of one generic strategy, a Personalized Visual Toolbox is a small collection of"
- "This course was never about one strategy. It was about building a system of support"
- "A visual schedule supports a transition."

nodes.title: Arc: the parent's own change, from overwhelmed and reactive to confident and proactive
nodes.description:
The book tracks the parent as closely as the child. The preface opens on parents left overwhelmed by strategies too clinical for real life, and Lesson 1 immediately offers a new identity, communication detective, in place of the passive wait for speech. Lesson 2's snapshot is framed to be non-judgmental, and Lesson 4 pauses the curriculum to make the parent celebrate successes of any size. Lesson 6 names the turn outright — no longer guessing — and the closing overview completes it as a move from reacting in the moment to anticipating, with a framework left over for problems the course never named.

Sources:
- "They need something real. Practical. Something they can use today."
- "you took an important step in moving from knowing about visual supports"
- "You may notice you’re moving from reacting in the moment to taking a more proactive"

nodes.title: Expressed goal: reduce the overwhelmed parent's cognitive load rather than add to it
nodes.description:
The design prompt makes load reduction a first-order requirement rather than a stylistic preference, naming the parent's existing state as the reason. The book's own content mostly honours this by refusing to hand the parent everything at once: Lesson 3 narrows fifteen visual support types to a single choice board, Lesson 4 picks one room instead of the whole house, and the closing overview cuts the whole toolkit down to one or two daily strategies. Where the goal strains is in the multi-step build procedures the later lessons assign. The emotional register the prompt asks for - warm, calm, spacious - is the same register the preface writes in, so voice and goal agree even where workload does not.

Sources:
- "Parents using this course may already be overwhelmed. The website should reduce cognitive load, not add"
- "Warm. Calm. Grounded. Spacious. Practical. Easy to return to."
- "Do not place the entire lesson on one endless webpage."

nodes.title: Expressed goal: something real and practical the parent can use today, not more theory
nodes.description:
The preface states the book's founding premise as a rejection of theory and long lists in favour of immediate usability, and the design prompt echoes it by making the Parent Activity one of the most important parts of each lesson and demanding the parent instantly know what to do, why, how long, and what is needed. The lessons deliver on this concretely and repeatedly: a five-second pause at the pantry, one quick fix in the kitchen today, giving a direction once and waiting. Each of those is executable in a single afternoon without materials. This is the goal the book meets most cleanly.

Sources:
- "They need something real. Practical. Something they can use today."
- "What am I doing? Why am I doing it? How long should it take? What do I need?"
- "Avoid making parents search through the lesson to find the activity."

nodes.title: Expressed goal: it should feel like Lolly walking alongside the parent, not a clinical or school portal
nodes.description:
The prompt sets the whole experience's voice as a person accompanying the parent and rules out the institutional, medical, and LMS registers by name. The preface and author note supply exactly that voice, ending on a direct promise of presence, and the autism primer deliberately cites the clinical definition only to set it aside as not reflecting daily life. The tension is that some lesson machinery - a scored knowledge check, a behaviours-per-minute calculation - carries the register the prompt banned, even when the surrounding prose is warm.

Sources:
- "The experience should feel like Lolly is gently walking alongside the parent through the course."
- "This is a parent education course, not a clinical learning portal and not a traditional online school."
- "I’ll be right here with you, each week, each lesson, each step."

nodes.title: Expressed goal: a resource to learn from, leave, return to, and keep using - not something to get through
nodes.description:
The prompt's core UX principle is explicitly anti-completion: the course should outlive the parent's pass through it, nothing should be locked, and returning should land the parent on Course Home with their place remembered. The book agrees at the level of structure, offering self-paced revisiting, an optional community, and three onward routes after the final lesson rather than a finish line. The frame unit's Course Home and the closing unit's keep-going goal are the two places this is directly implemented.

Sources:
- "It should feel like a resource they can learn from, leave, return to, and keep using."
- "Do not lock completed lessons. Parents should be able to revisit anything at any time."
- "You can move through it at your own pace, revisiting lessons as needed."

nodes.title: Expressed goal: never feel like the parent has opened a 150-page manual
nodes.description:
The prompt lists the 150-page manual as something to avoid, and the source it is describing is a 137-page course document, so this goal is a direct instruction about how to re-present the existing material. The prompt's remedy is structural - short sections, callouts, consistent lesson shape - and the book already supplies that shape in its repeating seven-part lesson structure. The moments that read most like a manual are the catalogue passages, such as Lesson 3's fifteen named support types, which the lesson itself immediately narrows to one board.

Sources:
- "like the parent has opened a 150-page manual"
- "Present the teaching content in short sections."
- "Consistency is important because parents should quickly learn how the course works."

nodes.title: Expressed goal: no points, badges, trophies or streaks - acknowledge progress simply and warmly
nodes.description:
The prompt bans gamified completion mechanics outright while still requiring visible progress and a marked lesson completion, so the distinction it draws is between tracking where you are and scoring how you are doing. The frame unit already encodes this as a rejected option. The book's own reward vocabulary - reinforcement, the Premack Principle, the star marker - is aimed at the child inside a routine, not at the parent inside the website, so it does not violate the prompt; the multiple-choice knowledge check is the one parent-facing element that edges toward being scored.

Sources:
- "Avoid gamification such as points, badges, trophies or streaks."
- "Acknowledge progress simply and warmly."
- "Your Progress Lesson X of 8 completed"

nodes.title: Expressed goal: design mobile-first, because many parents will read this on their phones
nodes.description:
The prompt is unambiguous that the phone is the primary device and sets concrete constraints: large buttons, readable text, obvious downloads, no pinch and zoom. This matters most for the parts of the course that are not reading at all - the printables. A mobile-first course whose deliverables are laminated boards and cut-out templates has to treat the phone as the place the parent decides and the printer as the place the work happens, which the prompt anticipates by insisting downloads stay obvious on small screens.

Sources:
- "Design mobile-first."
- "Many parents will access this course from their phones."
- "parents should never need to pinch and zoom"

nodes.title: Expressed goal: collect every tool in one place, organized by category rather than by lesson
nodes.description:
The prompt asks for a My Tools area so parents never have to remember which lesson held which printable, sorted into Communication, Routines and Transitions, Independence, and Preparing for Change, with each tool naming the lesson that teaches it. Those four categories map almost exactly onto the course's own arc, so the reorganisation is a re-index rather than a reinterpretation. The book independently reaches the same conclusion inside Lesson 5, where the parent is told to build a categorized, findable visual supports library at home - the site is doing for the parent what the course tells the parent to do for the family.

Sources:
- "Organize tools by category rather than only by lesson."
- "This should collect the practical resources from the course in one location so parents do not have to remember which lesson contained them."
- "Each tool should also indicate which lesson teaches parents how to use it."

nodes.title: Expressed goal: avoid feeling worksheet-heavy
nodes.description:
The prompt lists worksheet-heavy among the feelings to avoid, alongside institutional and clinical. This is the expressed goal in sharpest conflict with the source, because the course's practical spine is worksheets: checklists, tracking sheets, planning forms, templates, and the document's own first line names blackline masters as the material being edited. The prompt's own resolution is presentational rather than subtractive - keep the worksheets, but reach them through one obvious button and let simple ones be completed online so the printable is an option rather than the only route.

Sources:
- "worksheet-heavy"
- "Where worksheets are included, provide an obvious button:"
- "allow the parent to complete simple activities directly online while still offering a printable version."

nodes.title: Alignment: the book's one-small-step discipline is what actually delivers the low-load promise
nodes.description:
Across units the book repeatedly refuses to assign more than one thing, and this is the mechanism by which its content matches the prompt's calm, low-load ambition rather than merely its tone. Lesson 1 assigns observation only and explicitly withholds any change task; Lesson 3 asks the parent to just notice for a week; Lesson 4 converts a whole checklist into a single same-day fix; the closing overview rejects doing everything at once in favour of one or two strategies run daily. The preface names this as the design intent in its own words. Where the site can reinforce it, the Pause and Reflect framing is already written for it.

Sources:
- "These gentle, real-life activities are designed to help you put learning into practice, one small, manageable step at a time"
- "Each lesson offers bite-sized learning, simple activities, and real-life examples you can use right away."
- "Nothing needs to be fixed right now. This is a moment to notice."

nodes.title: Tension: the course is built on worksheets while the brief says not to feel worksheet-heavy
nodes.description:
Nearly every lesson's assigned work is a printed form - the Generalization Checklist, two communication tracking sheets, the Choice Board Planning Form, the Visual Environment Checklist, the Daily Routine and Transition Planning Chart, leveled IAS templates, the social story and comic strip templates. Removing them would remove the course's practical content, so the conflict cannot be resolved by deletion. It can only be resolved by presentation: a worksheet reached from a single obvious button at the moment it is needed, fillable on screen where it is simple, and otherwise discoverable later from My Tools rather than re-found by scrolling the lesson.

Sources:
- "Blackline masters: Week by week Editing N/A"
- "Printable visual tools you can start using right away"
- "Avoid making parents search through the lesson to find the activity."

nodes.title: Tension: several lessons ask for real preparation work against a goal of reducing load
nodes.description:
The later lessons escalate from noticing to building. Lesson 7's bin system is a nine-step setup from printed, cut and assembled templates; Lesson 6 asks the parent to build durable materials and then align other caregivers; Lesson 5 asks for anchor points, buffer time, a Top 3 and a stored, refreshed library; Lesson 4 walks a six-step timer introduction and a seven-level prompt hierarchy. Each is defensible on its own, but stacked they are the opposite of spacious. The prompt's four questions - what, why, how long, what do I need - are the mitigation: state the real time and materials cost up front for these lessons instead of letting a parent discover it mid-build.

Sources:
- "What am I doing? Why am I doing it? How long should it take? What do I need?"
- "They don’t need another long list of things to try."
- "This course is here to give you structure, support, and a sense of calm in the middle of the beautiful, messy work of parenting a child with autism."

nodes.title: Tension: Lesson 6's knowledge check is the one school-shaped element in a no-gamification course
nodes.description:
The prompt bans gamification and the LMS register, and the course mostly complies because its reward language points at the child, not the parent: reinforcement and the Premack Principle are things the parent does for the child inside a routine, and Lesson 8's star is a neutral schedule marker rather than an achievement token. The exception is Lesson 6's multiple-choice knowledge check, which is parent-facing and scored, and Lesson 4's celebrate-your-successes activity is the model for how the same beat should feel instead. If the check survives, it should read as self-orientation rather than assessment, with no score carried onto Course Home.

Sources:
- "Avoid gamification such as points, badges, trophies or streaks."
- "like an LMS or school portal"
- "Acknowledge progress simply and warmly."

nodes.title: Tension: Lesson 2's behaviours-per-minute calculation carries the clinical register the brief rules out
nodes.description:
Lesson 2's six-step observation ends in a calculated rate, which is the most measurement-shaped moment in the course and sits against a prompt that explicitly rejects the clinical learning portal and the medical feel. The book anticipates the problem itself, framing the number as a non-judgmental snapshot rather than a score, and the autism primer sets the same precedent by citing the clinical definition only to say it does not describe daily life. The site should carry that framing visually, treating the tracking sheets as noticing tools inside a quieter Pause and Reflect surface rather than as data entry.

Sources:
- "This is a parent education course, not a clinical learning portal and not a traditional online school."
- "But those clinical words don’t always reflect what day-to-day life looks like for a child"
- "Nothing needs to be fixed right now. This is a moment to notice."

nodes.title: Tension: family stories end in success while the brief forbids presenting examples as promised outcomes
nodes.description:
The prompt asks for family examples as warm, human story cards and states outright that they must not read as promises. Most of the course's stories resolve cleanly and quickly - the daughter moves from pointing to requesting, resistance softens within a week, communication starts getting results - which is exactly the shape the prompt warns against. Lesson 8's Poppy story is the counter-model the site should follow, because its reported result is honestly partial: still nervous, but no meltdown. Presenting the stories as one family's experience, and keeping the partial ones in, is what reconciles the two.

Sources:
- "Do not present examples as promises of outcomes."
- "Display family examples as warm story cards rather than long paragraphs."
- "Keep these human and relatable."

nodes.title: Tension: a mobile-first site delivering a course whose real output is printed, cut and laminated
nodes.description:
The course's deliverables are physical: printed and cut leveled templates, an All Done pocket, boards adapted for picture size and durability, labelled bins, a checklist walked around a room. A phone cannot produce any of those, so mobile-first here means the phone is where the parent reads, decides and finds the file, while the printer or the room is where the work lands. The prompt already accounts for this by demanding downloads stay obvious on small screens, and My Tools is the surface that lets a parent standing in their kitchen retrieve a template they first met three lessons ago.

Sources:
- "Design mobile-first."
- "worksheets and downloads should be obvious"
- "This section should become something parents continue returning to even after they finish the course."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lessons 1 and 4 print two different prompt hierarchies and never acknowledge the mismatch
nodes.description:
Lesson 1 teaches a five-level ladder (independent, model, gesture, partial physical, full physical) drawn as a pyramid with independence at the top, so fading is described as moving "upward." Lesson 4 prints a seven-level version numbered from full physical down to independent use, so fading is described as moving "down the hierarchy" — the same direction, the opposite spatial metaphor, for a parent who was told three lessons earlier to memorise the first one. Lesson 4 also inserts verbal and visual prompts between gesture and independence, which implies a verbal cue is less intrusive than a point, reversing the usual ordering, and its levels 4 and 6 are near-duplicates. This is the one place in Lessons 1-4 where the course's central technical tool is stated twice and inconsistently, and a parent tracking prompt levels across lessons cannot reconcile them.

Sources:
- "Prompts are arranged from the most independent at the top to the most supportive at the base."
- "As your child becomes more comfortable, gradually fade prompts by moving down the hierarchy."
- "Gesture Prompt: Point or tap near the visual." / "Visual Prompt: Point to the visual or use another cue."
