nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Errorless prompting applied to a choice board can have the parent choose the snack, not the child
nodes.description:
Errorless teaching is designed for tasks with a correct answer; a choice board has none, because the whole point is to surface what the child wants. Lesson 1 nevertheless runs the full ladder at the fridge board and ends at hand-over-hand, which means the parent physically moves the child's hand onto a card the parent picked — producing a "request" that carries no information about preference and teaching the child that an adult hand on theirs is part of the routine. Nothing in Lessons 1-4 distinguishes prompting a skill (touch the card) from prompting a choice (which card), or warns against physical prompting on a communication board specifically. Applied literally, the most supportive level of the hierarchy corrupts the exact signal the tool exists to collect.

Sources:
- "And if they still seem unsure, you could place your hand over theirs and help them make the choice (full physical)."
- "Guide their hand (if needed): Gently guide their hand while providing verbal reinforcement"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: "With ease" is the only stated criterion for fading a prompt, and Lesson 2 already holds the fix
nodes.description:
Lesson 1's instruction to step back a level fires on the phrase "with ease" — no count of consecutive independent responses, no across-days rule, no guidance on what to do after a regression. One lesson later the course hands the parent a Per Occurrence sheet whose columns are literally skill, prompt needed, and tally by time block, which is a prompt-fading data sheet in everything but name. The book never connects them: the tracking sheet is framed as a snapshot of communication frequency, not as the instrument that tells the parent when to drop from gesture to model. Joining those two pages would convert the course's vaguest instruction into its most concrete one at zero added cost to the parent.

Sources:
- "Once your child starts pointing with ease when given a gesture prompt, that's your cue to move to the next level, like simply modelling the action."
- "Prompt Needed? ... 1 gesture prompt ... Independent ... Model prompt"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The load-bearing 90%-nonverbal claim is the only major statistic in the course with no citation
nodes.description:
Lessons 3 and 4 cite Macdonald, Meaden, May, Arthur-Kelly, Ganz and Guhn, and the preface cites Cooper, Heron and Heward — so the course knows how to source a claim. The 90% figure, which is what licenses the entire communication-detective reframe, is asserted bare in Lesson 1 and re-asserted bare in Lesson 2. It descends from Mehrabian's experiments on judgments of attitude and feeling from mismatched cues, which is not a finding about the informational content of ordinary communication, and it is routinely overstated. The reframe survives without it; the number is doing rhetorical work the evidence does not support, and it sits in the one place a sceptical reader would check first.

Sources:
- "Here's something most people don't realize: Over 90% of communication is non-verbal."
- "It's important to remember that over 90% of communication is nonverbal."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: All eleven family stories in Lessons 1-4 succeed, and most resolve within days or weeks
nodes.description:
Sasha, Jared, Anika, Mateo, Alex and Jack, Sam and Leo, Karen, the nightstand family, Raj, William, Liam and Mark all end in a win, usually with an explicit short timeline. There is no story in these four lessons where a child ignores the board, destroys it, points at random, or where the parent gives up and restarts — the only acknowledgement that visuals get chewed and thrown is tucked into Lesson 3's optional Facebook section, outside the teaching. The selection converts "worth trying" into "works," which matters for an audience the preface defines by prior failed strategies: a parent whose first board does nothing for a month has no modelled version of their own experience and will read the non-response as their own error. Lesson 8's Poppy story (still nervous, no meltdown) shows the book can tell a partial win; the early lessons simply do not.

Sources:
- "Within a couple of weeks, she started pointing to the card on her own, no more accidents."
- "Now, snack time is a calm, connected routine regardless of who is with him"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: "In sight but out of reach" is mand training presented as a decluttering tip
nodes.description:
Lesson 4 files visible storage under organisation, but placing a wanted item where the child can see it and not get it is a deliberate contrivance of motivation — the standard behaviour-analytic move for manufacturing a request opportunity. The "request station" fix says so outright: the goldfish move from a dark pantry to a clear jar on the counter precisely so the child must ask. Naming the mechanism would help the parent apply it well; leaving it unnamed means the parent gets the arrangement without the conditions that make it humane, namely that the request is honoured fast and that the setup is dropped when the child is already dysregulated. A tired parent who installs the clear jar and then is slow or inconsistent has built a frustration generator, not a communication opportunity.

Sources:
- "Start by keeping things in sight but out of reach."
- "Create a Request Station: Move the goldfish crackers from the dark pantry to a clear jar on the counter."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The five-second pause is called the simplest strategy but is only modelled during calm moments
nodes.description:
Lesson 2 offers silent counting to five as the course's easiest intervention, and it is the right mechanism for a processing delay. But the scenes the course uses to recruit the parent are escalations — the 4:45 fridge, the rising heart rate, the building meltdown — and holding five seconds of silence in front of a child who is already crying is neither simple nor obviously correct. Lessons 1 through 4 never distinguish waiting during a neutral request from waiting during escalation, and never say when to abandon the pause and just meet the need. The parent is left to discover the difference on the worst possible occasion.

Sources:
- "One of the most effective strategies is also one of the simplest: pause. Giving your child a few extra seconds, perhaps counting to five silently, allows them the time they need to understand and respond."
- "The whining escalates. You feel your heart rate rising."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lesson 2's behaviours-per-minute baseline is sampled under best-case conditions it never asks to replicate
nodes.description:
Step 1 tells the parent to observe when the child is alert or engaged, and Step 5 frames the resulting rate as a snapshot to compare growth against later. Those two instructions conflict: a rate drawn from a deliberately favourable five-to-fifteen minute window is a ceiling measure, and unless the parent records the activity, time of day, people present and duration and reproduces them, the next sample is measuring a different situation. The book supplies no place on either sheet for those conditions and never tells the parent to hold them constant. The predictable failure is a second observation that reads as regression when only the setting changed — the exact misreading Lesson 1 spends pages warning against.

Sources:
- "Pick a time when your child is alert or engaged"
- "This isn't about scoring your child. It's just about getting a snapshot of today so you can notice growth later."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lessons 2-4 install exactly the narrow cue-dependence Lesson 1 diagnosed as the core problem
nodes.description:
Lesson 1's account of generalization failure is that autistic learners bind skills to very specific cues — this room, this person, these materials — and lose the skill when the cues change. Lessons 2 through 4 then prescribe laminating a shoe picture for this front door, a board for this fridge, a chart for this sink, and Lesson 3 makes cue-locality an explicit design rule. That is the right first move and also, by the book's own theory, the construction of a new cue dependence. Lesson 1 lists practice in multiple settings as a support, but no lesson in 1-4 gives a procedure for duplicating a board to a second location, moving it, or thinning it; Jared's story quietly does it by using the same card at daycare and home, and the book never lifts that into a method.

Sources:
- "Children with autism often rely heavily on very specific cues. What room they're in, who's with them, or what materials are being used. When those cues change, they may no longer recognize that the skill still applies."
- "Placement Matters: Place visuals where they'll be used, like a handwashing chart near the sink or a bedtime routine in the bedroom."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: "Communication gets results" assumes every board request is granted, and Lessons 1-4 never handle refusal
nodes.description:
Lesson 3's worked example puts a picture of ice cream on the freezer so the child can request it, and concludes that this teaches the child communication gets results. Every choice-board example in these lessons is built from items the parent already intends to hand over. The course never addresses the ice cream at 7am, the twentieth request in an hour, or the item that has run out — and by its own reinforcement logic, a board honoured inconsistently teaches that requesting is unreliable, which is worse than no board, because the meltdown still works. The fix is small (only picture what is genuinely available, and pair refusal with a first-then or an all-done card) and its absence is the most likely practical failure of a parent's first week.

Sources:
- "If your child sees ice cream in the freezer and begins to tantrum because they can't express their desire, a picture of ice cream on the freezer provides a simple way to make a request. Over time, this teaches them that communication gets results."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Liam's emotion chart demonstrates an endpoint of teaching the course never provides
nodes.description:
The emotion chart appears in Lesson 3's menu of fifteen, then in a family story where Liam already scans the chart, identifies anger, and later starts using it before he escalates. Identifying and labelling an internal state is categorically harder than selecting a preferred snack — it requires interoception, symbolic mapping of a face to a feeling, and doing all of it while dysregulated — and the lesson's own decision is to start with a single snack, toy or book board. Nothing in Lessons 1-4 teaches the intermediate steps, so the story reads as achievable when it depicts months of work. A parent who prints an emotion chart on the strength of this vignette is likely to conclude the tool failed.

Sources:
- "She gently said, "Can you show me how you feel?" and pointed to the pictures. Liam looked at the chart and pointed to the angry face."
- "Start by choosing one small moment in your day where your child usually needs to make a choice."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Reassurance substitutes for troubleshooting: Lessons 1-4 never say what to do when a tool does not work
nodes.description:
The early lessons repeatedly remove the possibility of failure — no right or wrong answers, the goal is not to get it perfect, progress is progress — and Lesson 4's entire parent activity is to celebrate what you already did. That warmth is genuinely well judged for an audience defined by overwhelm, but it is also carrying structural weight: because nothing can be done wrong, the course never has to specify what success looks like or what the parent should change when a board is ignored for two weeks. The first real diagnostic content is Lesson 6's wrong-tool-not-broken-strategy move, which lands three lessons after the parent was told to install a board. A single "if this isn't working after a week, try this" box in Lessons 3 and 4 would cost the tone nothing.

Sources:
- "Note: There are no right or wrong answers here. This is about noticing patterns, not fixing anything just yet."
- "This week, take time to recognize what you've already accomplished. Whether you cleared out a drawer, set up a snack station, or introduced your first visual schedule, it matters. Progress is progress."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Real strength: Lesson 1 assigns no change task at all, and that is a retention decision as much as a teaching one
nodes.description:
The first lesson of a course sold to exhausted parents asks for ten to fifteen minutes of watching and explicitly forbids fixing anything. For readers who arrive having already failed at other people's strategies, an opening assignment with no failure condition is the cheapest possible re-entry, and it buys two things at once: the parent practises the observation stance the rest of the course depends on, and the resulting worksheet becomes the comparison point Lesson 2 measures against. Most parent-education material spends its first lesson proving value by prescribing an action; withholding the action here is the more sophisticated move and is easy to mistake for a slow start.

Sources:
- "Before we start making changes, let's take a moment to observe your child's environment as it is today."
- "Note: There are no right or wrong answers here. This is about noticing patterns, not fixing anything just yet."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lesson 4's opening scene describes a request its own prescribed tools would have missed
nodes.description:
The child in the 4:30 kitchen wanted the blue bowl they use for grapes — a specific container, not a food category. Clear containers, a decluttered counter and a three-picture snack board of crackers, yogurt and banana do not represent that request; the board would have offered the wrong dimension entirely. The book's own best-observed vignette is therefore a case where the lesson's tools fail, which points at a real limitation it never names: choice boards encode the categories the parent anticipated, and many requests are about specificity (this cup, this route, this order) rather than selection. Lesson 3 gestures at the remedy when it suggests real photos of the child's actual items, but never links it back to this problem.

Sources:
- "By the time you realize they were actually looking for the blue bowl they use for grapes, everyone is exhausted."
- "In some cases, real photos of your child's actual items (their cup, favourite snack, or specific toy) may be easier to recognize than stock images or icons."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Real strength: redefining "behaviour" before any tool appears is what makes Lesson 2's tracking sheet usable
nodes.description:
Lesson 1 spends a short aside redefining behaviour as anything a person does, including stillness. It looks like terminology housekeeping and it is actually the hinge: without it, Lesson 2's tracking sheet reads as an incident log and the parent records only the screaming. With it, a look, a pause and a hand-pull become countable entries, which is the difference between a communication baseline and a behaviour-problem diary. Placing the definition before the instrument rather than alongside it is the reason the six-step observation can be framed as non-judgmental without that framing being merely a tone choice.

Sources:
- "In the field of behaviour analysis, behaviour simply means anything a person does, including communication, gestures, choices, movements, and even stillness."
- "These are all meaningful forms of communication, even if they don't involve words yet."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The nonverbal-communication statistic drifts between lessons and cites nothing
nodes.description:
Lesson 1 builds the communication-detective reframe on the claim that over 90% of communication is non-verbal; Lesson 5 restates the same load-bearing claim as "around 80%" and hedges it to "some studies suggest" without naming one. Both figures descend from Mehrabian's 1967 studies of single-word vocal tone, which measured how listeners resolve conflicting affective cues and were never a finding about communication in general. The drift matters because the number is doing argumentative work in two separate places, and a parent who notices the inconsistency has no way to check either version. The teaching survives without the statistic — a child who cannot speak is obviously communicating some other way — so citing it is a rhetorical choice that adds a falsifiable claim the book does not need.

Sources:
- "Most communication is actually nonverbal, some studies suggest around 80%, and children with autism often need a little extra time to process verbal instructions."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: First-Then boards run for four lessons before Lesson 6 explains why they work
nodes.description:
The First-Then board is placed in the home in Lesson 2, used to rescue the blocks-to-dinner transition in Lesson 5, and named as a toolbox staple throughout — but the mechanism that makes it work, the Premack Principle, is not taught until Lesson 6. Lesson 5 comes within one sentence of it ("we were careful to make sure the 'Then' was motivating") and then leaves the parent to infer the rule rather than stating it. A parent who builds a First-Then board in week 2 with an unmotivating "Then" will conclude the tool is broken, which is exactly the misdiagnosis Lesson 6 exists to correct. Moving one paragraph of Lesson 6 forward to Lesson 2 would cost nothing and would prevent the most likely early failure.

Sources:
- "But we were careful to make sure the 'Then' was motivating"
- "The Premack Principle is a simple strategy that helps children complete less-preferred tasks by pairing them with something they enjoy."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lesson 6 rests on a diagnostic skill it teaches in one sentence
nodes.description:
The whole lesson turns on a single question the parent must answer mid-transition about a child who may not be able to explain anything: is this refusal about choosing, or about not knowing the steps? That is a differential diagnosis of an internal state, and Lessons 1 through 5 never teach it. What they teach is frequency observation — Lesson 2's six-step count produces a behaviours-per-minute rate, which measures how often communication happens and is silent on why a support failed. The gap shows in the guidance offered: "Refusal? Confusion? Meltdown?" are three surface presentations of a child in distress, not three distinguishable causes, and the lesson gives no procedure for telling them apart.

Sources:
- "Is my child struggling with making a choice… or with understanding what to do?"
- "What kind of challenge is happening? (Refusal? Confusion? Meltdown?)"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Every back-half family story resolves, and each one names a short timeline
nodes.description:
Lessons 5 through 8 contain seven family examples and all seven end in improvement, six of them with an explicit clock attached: within a week, within days, within two weeks. There is no story of a tool that took three months, no story of a family who tried the bin system and found their child dismantled it, no story of a support abandoned. The selection is doing quiet work the text never claims outright — it sets the parent's expected time-to-payoff at one to two weeks, so a parent at week four with no change has been given no model of themselves. Jason is the closest thing to a failure case, and even there the failure is instantly corrected by the right tool and resolved "within days".

Sources:
- "Within a week, the resistance softened, and transitions started to feel a little less charged."
- "At first, she sat beside her son during the entire schedule. Within two weeks, he was completing both activities without her prompting!"
- "Within days, things shifted. Less resistance. More independence. A smoother start to the day."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Poppy's "still nervous, but no meltdown" is the only calibrated result in the course
nodes.description:
Against the pattern of clean resolutions, the haircut story reports a partial win and names the residue: the child was still anxious. This is the single most useful sentence in the back half, because it hands the parent a realistic success criterion — the goal was never a child who enjoys haircuts, it was a haircut that ends without a collapse. It also implicitly licenses the parent to count a hard-but-survivable outing as the strategy working. The strength is easy to miss precisely because it is one line in one story, and nothing in the surrounding text points at it or generalises it into a rule.

Sources:
- "The result? Still a little nervous, but no meltdown. More cooperation. A big step forward."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The star marks both the dentist and ice cream, so it teaches a coin flip
nodes.description:
Lesson 8 defines the star as neutral and then immediately scripts the parent to announce it as "different or special", and the worked list pairs it with dentist, haircut and grandma visiting alongside park and ice cream after school. A symbol whose referent set spans a dental appointment and a treat cannot be neutral in practice; it becomes a gamble the child is asked to resolve every time it appears. For an anxious child the likely learning is that the star predicts uncertainty, which is the exact state the tool was introduced to reduce. The fix is available inside the book's own logic — the star is always paired with a picture of the actual change — but the text presents that pairing as Step 3 of building up to bigger changes rather than as a rule that must hold from the first use.

Sources:
- "The ⭐ is: Positive, Neutral (not scary!), A signal that something is a little different"
- "You might say: 'Oh look! A star today. Something different or special is happening.'"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lesson 8 spends the trust that Lessons 4-7 built into the schedule
nodes.description:
Lessons 4 through 7 earn the visual schedule its authority by making it invariant: the same cues every day, items in consistent places, bins in the same order. Lesson 8 then deliberately inserts a change marker into that surface, which is a coherent design — the trusted object is the only safe place to deliver bad news — but it is also a withdrawal from an account the parent spent four weeks funding. The book never names this cost or the failure mode it creates: if early stars land on genuinely aversive events, the schedule itself becomes a thing the child avoids checking, and every downstream tool that depends on it degrades at once. Introducing the star inside a known routine with a trivially small change is the right mitigation, and the text does say to do it; it just does not say what is being protected or what happens if the sequencing is rushed.

Sources:
- "Place the ⭐ within a routine your child already knows well, like setting the table, to introduce change in a simple and manageable way."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The mastered-tasks-only rule is Lesson 7's strongest and least obvious move
nodes.description:
Filling the bins with activities the child already knows isolates the single variable being taught — following the schedule — so any failure is unambiguously a schedule problem rather than a task problem. That is proper instructional design, and it is the one place in the course where a rule is stated with a reason attached rather than as a tip. It also quietly forbids the most tempting parental shortcut, which is to use the new structure to finally get the child to practise the hard thing. The unexamined consequence is that the parent now needs an inventory of genuinely mastered, self-terminating activities, and nothing in Lessons 1 to 6 asked them to build one: Lesson 1's observation homework catalogues communication, not task competence.

Sources:
- "When starting an IAS, it is best to use mastered tasks, things the person already knows how to do. The goal is to teach the process of following the schedule, not to teach a brand-new skill."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The IAS has no fading procedure and no criterion for moving up a level
nodes.description:
Lesson 7's whole purpose is independence, yet the nine-step setup ends at "guide your child through each activity" and never describes how the parent withdraws. Karla's story carries the entire fading procedure implicitly — she sat beside her son, and two weeks later she was not — but how she stopped sitting there is exactly the thing not told. Lessons 1 and 4 taught explicit prompt hierarchies for precisely this, and Lesson 7 does not reference either, so the course's central technique goes unused at the moment it matters most. The same absence governs the leveled templates: "confidence first, complexity later" is a sentiment, not a criterion, and no number of independent runs is ever named as the threshold for moving from colour matching to numbers to written words.

Sources:
- "Step 6. Guide the Routine: Guide your child through each activity, allowing them to complete parts of the routine independently (like completing the actual activity)"
- "Always move at your child's pace, confidence first, complexity later!"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lesson 7 is the course's most materially expensive week, against a low-load promise
nodes.description:
The bin system needs two or three matching bins, a printer, scissors, laminate or cardstock, Velcro, an All Done pocket, a designated schedule surface and numbered workstations — assembled before the child sees any of it. That is a shopping trip and an evening of cutting, asked of the same parent the frame described as overwhelmed and asked for something usable today. It is also the sharpest instance of the mobile-first tension: nothing about this lesson can be done on a phone, and the phone's only role is to hold the templates that must be printed. The course's own one-small-step discipline is suspended here, and nothing in the lesson offers a cheaper first version, such as running the sequence with three existing household containers and hand-drawn cards before committing to materials.

Sources:
- "Step 2: Set Up Bins: Get 2 or 3 identical bins or trays, place one activity in each bin"
- "Print and assemble materials using durable methods such as laminating, cardstock, or taping."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The Power of Silence has no branch for the child who does not move
nodes.description:
Lesson 5's assignment is to give the direction once and wait, and the only worked example is Lisa, whose daughter starts moving after the pause. The lesson tells the parent the pause will feel long and to sit with the discomfort, but never names an upper bound or what to do at the far end of it. Without that, the technique has two failure modes the text does not distinguish: waiting too little, which is the error it targets, and waiting past the point where the child has disengaged and the demand has simply gone unanswered. The answer already exists elsewhere in the course — after the pause, move down the prompting hierarchy from Lesson 1 or 4 — and Lesson 5 makes no link to it, so "wait" is left as the terminal instruction.

Sources:
- "Try this: give the instruction just once, then pause."
- "The pause may feel long to you, but for your child, it can be the space they need to respond."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lesson 7's evidence section cites databases, not studies
nodes.description:
Lessons 5 and 6 cite in a conventional author-date form that a reader could chase: Howlin et al. 2017, Mundy et al. 2007, Premack 1959, Dettmer et al. 2000, McCabe 2020. Lesson 7, which carries the course's strongest empirical claim, attributes a meta-analysis to "(ERIC, ResearchGate)" and a transition finding to "(Sage Journals, ResearchGate)" — these are repositories and a publisher, not sources, and they identify no study, author or year. This is the one place where the book's warmth is standing in for rigour in a way a reader can catch: the sentence performs the gesture of citation while supplying nothing checkable. Activity schedules genuinely do have a supporting literature, so the cost here is credibility rather than accuracy.

Sources:
- "A meta-analysis found significant improvements in independent behaviours and task engagement among children using IAS (ERIC, ResearchGate)."
- "Visual schedules help smooth transitions between activities, improving classroom behavior and decreasing anxiety (Sage Journals, ResearchGate)."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lessons 5-8 give no stop rule; "stay consistent" is the only answer to no response
nodes.description:
Every lesson in the back half closes on persistence, and none defines how long persistence is supposed to last or what evidence would justify abandoning a plan. Lesson 6 looks like the exception but is not: its diagnostic trigger is an acute event, the child visibly upset at a transition, and it offers nothing for the far more common case of a support that produces neither distress nor change over weeks. The result is an asymmetry — the course is precise about setup, with nine numbered steps for a bin system, and entirely unspecific about review. A parent running a failing IAS has been told in advance that change takes time, which makes their own accumulating evidence look like impatience.

Sources:
- "Change takes time! Stick to the plan consistently to help your child develop new habits. With patience, persistence, and the right support, you're setting them up for success."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lesson 8 teaches rehearsable change only, not the unplanned kind that actually hurts
nodes.description:
Every example in the lesson is a change the parent knows about days in advance and can prepare for: dentist, haircut, a visitor, starting school, an outing, ice cream after school. The core procedure requires that lead time by construction — read the story once a day for several days before the event, in a calm moment. But the changes that produce the hardest days are the ones with no notice: a cancelled plan, a closed playground, a substitute teacher, a broken favourite object. The course therefore ends having taught predictable unpredictability, and the parent's framework for genuine surprise is whatever transfer the child manages on their own from the rehearsed cases.

Sources:
- "Review the social story when your child is calm, not in the middle of the stressful moment. Read it together once a day for a few days leading up to the event if possible."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The closing keeps two of fifteen tools and offers no criterion for choosing
nodes.description:
The overview layers seven domains and the course has introduced something like fifteen named supports, and then the maintenance plan is one or two strategies run daily. That is the most honest advice in the book — it accepts that a sustained small practice beats an abandoned large one — but it also means the closing openly designs most of the course to be dropped, and it does not help with the drop. The reflection questions ask what felt most helpful, which surfaces the parent's retrospective preference rather than a fit between tool and problem. Lesson 6 already built the selection discipline that could answer this properly (what kind of challenge is happening, is this structure or choice), and the overview does not reach back for it.

Sources:
- "What matters most is not doing everything at once, or doing it perfectly, but choosing what works, staying consistent, and allowing those small changes to build over time."
- "Choose one or two strategies that felt most helpful and continue using them daily"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The overview ends a reflection week with a quiz
nodes.description:
The closing parent activity explicitly lowers the demand — keep it simple, you don't need to do everything — and then, two lines later, sets a graded course quiz. This is the second test in three lessons, after Lesson 6's multiple-choice knowledge check, and it puts the course's final impression in a school register the design brief rules out. The mismatch is not just tonal: a reflection week asks the parent to notice what changed at home, while a quiz asks whether they retained the book, and only one of those is evidence the course worked. Replacing it with the reflection questions already on the page would cost nothing and would leave the parent holding their own observations rather than a score.

Sources:
- "This week is about reflection. Keep it simple. You don't need to do everything, just keep going."
- "Now try to complete this short quiz based on the course:"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The nonverbal-communication statistic is uncited and the book contradicts itself
nodes.description:
The founding reframe rests on a number the book cannot keep steady: Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 both assert "over 90%" of communication is non-verbal, while Lesson 5 says "around 80%" and attributes it vaguely to "some studies". Neither figure carries a citation, and both trace back to the Mehrabian ratio, which was derived from single-word affect judgments in a lab and was never a claim about informational content. This matters more than a pedantic correction because the statistic is doing argumentative work: it is the warrant for the whole move from listening for speech to reading behaviour. The reframe is defensible on its own terms for autistic communication specifically, and would be stronger stated that way than propped on a borrowed number the book itself reports two ways.

Sources:
- "Here's something most people don't realize: Over 90% of communication is non-verbal."
- "Most communication is actually nonverbal, some studies suggest around 80%, and children with autism often need a little extra time to process verbal instructions."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: A behaviour-analytic course that never teaches the function of behaviour
nodes.description:
The author is a behaviour specialist and the primer cites Cooper, Heron and Heward, yet across 137 pages the course never teaches that behaviour has a function — escape, access, attention, sensory. The word "antecedent" appears exactly twice in the whole book, both times as an unexplained column header on Lesson 2's sample tracking sheet, and the six-step observation counts behaviours and divides by minutes without ever asking what the behaviour achieves. The consequence is concrete: a parent taught only "behaviour is communication" will read escape-motivated refusal as an unmet request and keep adding visuals to a problem visuals do not address, then conclude the tool is broken. Lesson 6 later requires exactly this missing analysis.

Sources:
- "(Antecedent)          (Communication)"
- "Total behaviours observed ÷ Minutes observed = Behaviours per minute"
- "As Cooper et al. emphasize, promoting skill generalization and building meaningful communication involves strategic prompting, reinforcement, and environmental design"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: No lesson has an if-this-doesn't-work branch
nodes.description:
Every lesson runs a single happy path: place the support, model it, fade the prompt, get the result. There is no troubleshooting section anywhere in the book — no guidance for the child who ignores the board, tears the schedule off the wall on day three, or complies for a week and then stops. The one honest partial result in the whole course is Poppy, and it is reported as an ending rather than used to teach what to do next. A parent whose first choice board fails has been handed nothing except Lesson 6's advice to try a different tool, which arrives five weeks later.

Sources:
- "The result? Still a little nervous, but no meltdown. More cooperation. A big step forward."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Every family story succeeds, most within days, which functions as a promise
nodes.description:
Roughly fifteen family vignettes appear across the eight lessons and not one ends in failure, abandonment, or a tool that had to be dropped. The recurring cadence is a compressed timeline plus a three-beat payoff — "Within days, things shifted. Less resistance. More independence." — which is the rhetorical shape of a testimonial, not a case study. The design prompt explicitly forbids presenting examples as promises of outcomes, but that constraint is about the prose, not the card styling: restyling these as warm story cards leaves the promise fully intact. The cheapest honest fix is one story per course that did not work and what the family changed.

Sources:
- "Within days, things shifted. Less resistance. More independence. A smoother start to the day."
- "Within a week, the resistance softened, and transitions started to feel a little less charged."
- "Do not present examples as promises of outcomes."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lesson 6 asks for a differential diagnosis that Lessons 1 to 5 never teach
nodes.description:
Lesson 6's entire method turns on the parent answering two questions in the moment: what kind of challenge is this (refusal, confusion, meltdown), and is the child missing structure or missing choice. Nothing earlier in the course teaches that distinction. Lesson 2 teaches counting communicative acts, Lesson 3 teaches board construction, Lessons 4 and 5 teach placement and sequencing — none teach reading an escalation curve or separating cognitive overload from decision load. Jason gets the diagnosis right because he "paused and looked closer", which narrates the skill rather than teaching it, and leaves the parent's success dependent on intuition the course claims not to require.

Sources:
- "What kind of challenge is happening? (Refusal? Confusion? Meltdown?)"
- "His son wasn't stuck on choosing; he was overwhelmed by the steps."
- "You don't need to be a therapist, a teacher, or a behaviour expert to help your child learn to communicate."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The real weekly cost is craft labour, and no lesson ever budgets it
nodes.description:
By the end of the course the parent has been asked to print, cut, laminate, velcro, mount and file: a choice board, two tracking sheets, an environment checklist, a visual schedule, a First-Then board, a timer routine, a planning chart, a four-tool toolbox, leveled IAS templates with matched bin markers and an All Done pocket, a social story, and a comic template. That is a sustained craft project, and the book never states a minutes-per-week figure for any of it. The design prompt's Parent Activity section asks the site to answer "How long should it take?", a question the source material does not answer anywhere. This is the sharpest version of the load tension: the overwhelmed parent the preface diagnoses is handed a laminator.

Sources:
- "Print and assemble materials using durable methods such as laminating, cardstock,"
- "Step 3: Create the Schedule: Using our IAS templates below, print, cut and make the visual schedule most appropriate for your child."
- "Parents using this course may already be overwhelmed. The website should reduce cognitive load, not add to it."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: No AAC, no speech-language referral, and no stated ceiling on what home visuals can do
nodes.description:
The words AAC, PECS, speech-language pathologist, communication device and augmentative do not appear once in the book, and there is no referral guidance of any kind — no "if your child is doing X, talk to a professional". For a course explicitly aimed at families of children who do not yet speak, laminated picture cards are presented as the top of the ladder when for many of these children they are the bottom rung of a formal AAC pathway. The same gap covers risk: self-injury and aggression are never mentioned, so a parent whose child's meltdowns include either is given only "read it as communication" and no threshold for seeking help. A single honest page on scope and escalation would cost the book nothing and remove a real liability.

Sources:
- "Children with autism often learn best through consistent, structured, visual, and hands-on supports."
- "You don't need to be a therapist, a teacher, or a behaviour expert to help your child learn to communicate."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Eleven of Lesson 3's fifteen visual supports are named once and never taught
nodes.description:
Lesson 3 catalogues fifteen support types, then the remainder of the course develops four or five — choice boards, visual schedules, First-Then boards, timers, social stories. Object cues, communication boards, transition cards, task strips, routine charts, rule reminders and token charts are named, defined in a half-line, and dropped. The list is doing display work — it signals the field's breadth and the author's command of it — but its residue on the reader is a set of tool names they now believe exist for their child and cannot build. Narrowing to one board is the right call; the honest version says which eleven are out of scope and why, instead of listing them and walking away.

Sources:
- "●​ Object cues-using real objects to represent an activity (e.g., a spoon for snack time)"
- "●​ Token or reward charts- track progress toward a reward or goal"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The worksheets are not an accessory to the course, they are the course
nodes.description:
The existing alignment note treats worksheet-heaviness as a tension to be managed; it is stronger than that. In seven of eight lessons the Parent Activity IS the worksheet — the Generalization Checklist, the Communication Tracking Sheet, the Visual Environment Checklist, the Daily Routine and Transition Planning Chart, the toolbox build, the IAS templates, the social story outline. Remove the worksheets and the course is eight essays with no assigned work. So the design prompt's "avoid worksheet-heavy" cannot be satisfied by the content, only by the packaging: the site can present the same instruments as guided, one-question-at-a-time interactions with a printable fallback, or it can feel like a workbook. There is no third option, and the build should decide this deliberately rather than discover it.

Sources:
- "Avoid anything that feels: ... worksheet-heavy"
- "Where worksheets are included, provide an obvious button:"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The closing overview contains a second quiz, so the course bookends with tests
nodes.description:
The graph's alignment note calls Lesson 6's knowledge check the one school-shaped element in a no-gamification course; that undercounts. The closing overview also drops a quiz in — "Now try to complete this short quiz based on the course" — placed between the reflection activity and the extension workbook pitch, with no framing and no stated purpose. Two graded-feeling instruments, one at the two-thirds mark and one at the finish, is a pattern rather than an outlier, and it pulls directly against a design brief that bans points, badges and streaks and against the book's own repeated "this isn't a test". The product decision is whether to render both as self-check reflection or cut the closing one.

Sources:
- "Now try to complete this short quiz based on the course:"
- "Avoid gamification such as points, badges, trophies or streaks."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Lesson 2 builds a baseline rate and no later lesson ever measures again
nodes.description:
Lesson 2 teaches the parent to define a behaviour, count instances, divide by minutes, and explicitly frames the number as a snapshot "so you can notice growth later". Later never arrives. No subsequent lesson asks the parent to re-run the observation, and the closing reflection week asks "What feels different now compared to when you started?" — a memory question, answered six weeks after the one objective measurement the course ever produced. This is the single cheapest structural fix available: reinstate the Lesson 2 observation in the closing week and the course acquires a real before-and-after, plus a non-anecdotal answer when a parent feels nothing has changed.

Sources:
- "This isn't about scoring your child. It's just about getting a snapshot of today so you can notice growth later."
- "What feels different now compared to when you started?"

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: A weekly cadence outruns the generalization timeline the book itself teaches
nodes.description:
Lesson 1 establishes that skills take time to travel across people, places and things and warns against reading the lag as regression. The course structure then contradicts that pacing: eight weekly lessons, each introducing a new tool while the previous week's is still in its first days of use, so by Lesson 7 the parent is building bins for a child whose Lesson 3 choice board may be two weeks old. The book knows this — the closing overview says do not do everything at once — but it says it in week nine, after the accumulation has already happened. Front-loading that instruction, or explicitly designating consolidation weeks, would cost nothing and would let the eight-lesson sequence survive a hard week instead of generating guilt about falling behind.

Sources:
- "This isn't regression. It's simply a sign that generalization hasn't happened yet."
- "What matters most is not doing everything at once, or doing it perfectly, but choosing what works, staying consistent, and allowing those small changes to build over time."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: Warmth and a citation-shaped apparatus stand in where rigour would sit
nodes.description:
The book's evidence layer is decorative in places rather than load-bearing. Lesson 7 cites a meta-analysis to "(ERIC, ResearchGate)" and a claim about anxiety to "(Sage Journals, ResearchGate)" — those are a database and a repository, not sources, and cannot be checked. Lesson 2 opens a paragraph with "Research shows that children on the spectrum often need more chances to initiate" and cites nothing. Elsewhere real citations appear (Ganz 2007, Dettmer et al. 2000, Mundy et al. 2007) so the author clearly can do this. The warmth then finishes the job the citations start: a reader who trusts Lolly does not audit the reference, and the twenty-five years and thousand families are what actually carry the claims. That is a working rhetorical system and it is also the reason nothing in the book gets challenged.

Sources:
- "A meta-analysis found significant improvements in independent behaviours and task engagement among children using IAS (ERIC, ResearchGate)."
- "Research shows that children on the spectrum often need more chances to initiate or start communication."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The course's strongest moves are its refusals, and they are the easiest to cut
nodes.description:
Three of the best decisions in the book are things it declines to do. Lesson 1 assigns no change task at all — ten to fifteen minutes of watching, nothing to fix — which is the single most protective instruction in the course for a parent who has been thrashing. Lesson 7 rules out using the Independent Activity Schedule to teach a new skill, correctly separating schedule-following from task acquisition. The closing overview refuses the whole toolkit in favour of one or two strategies kept daily. All three read as thin lessons on a product spreadsheet — a week with no deliverable, a restriction, a shrinking scope — which makes them the first casualties of any pass that optimises perceived value per lesson. They should be protected explicitly in the build.

- "Choose 2–3 simple activities your child enjoys."

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The assumed reader is one adult with a quiet hour and full control of the home
nodes.description:
The activities silently require conditions many of these households do not have: an uninterrupted ten to fifteen minutes to observe one child, a daily practice session for the IAS, calm moments to introduce new visuals, and the authority to relabel the kitchen and rearrange storage. Siblings appear only as generalization targets, never as the reason the observation gets abandoned. Shared custody, rentals, grandparents' houses and daycare are absent, even though the course's whole theory is environmental — a strategy that fails the moment the child spends three nights a week in a home nobody has labelled. The one concession to reality is genuinely good and stands almost alone: set your phone on a shelf if you are parenting solo.

nodes.title: AI_NOTE: The book's decisions are staged as binaries whose losing side is a strawman parent
nodes.description:
Nearly every decision point in this graph inherits a rhetorical device from the text: a two-option choice where the rejected option is a caricature of what the reader is presumed to be doing wrong. The pantry moment is quick-fix-snack versus picture-and-pause; Lesson 1 is errorless prompting versus letting the child fail; Lesson 3 is a choice board versus repeating yourself louder; Lesson 5 is silence versus nagging. Real alternatives never appear — sign, a device, teaching the vocal approximation, or simply answering the child's hand-pull, which is already successful communication the book elsewhere insists we honour. The graph faithfully records these as options, which makes it look like the book weighed alternatives when it mostly staged them. Readers of the graph should treat the rejected branches as motivational framing, not as deliberation.

themes.name: behaviour-is-communication
themes.description: The book's founding reframe: nothing a child does is meaningless, and a meltdown, a hand-pull or a scream at the fridge is a message being sent with the only equipment available. It asks the parent to stop measuring communication in spoken words and to read the non-verbal 90% instead, which converts 'behaviour problems' into unanswered requests. It is stated in the frame (social communication differences, repetitive behaviour as coping not defect), dramatised in Lesson 1's fridge meltdown and Lesson 2's pantry and park scenes, and returns in Lesson 3's yogurt and emotion-chart material and Les

themes.name: change-the-environment-not-the-child
themes.description: When a skill does not appear, the book's reflex is to alter the room rather than revise the verdict on the child: move the snack into a clear jar, put a picture by the door, label the bin. The claim is that most home failures are design failures, so the parent's lever is arrangement, not correction or willpower. Lesson 1 makes the choice explicit ('change the environment rather than the verdict on the child'), Lesson 2 places the first supports where routines actually happen, and Lesson 4 gives the whole argument a room-by-room method.

themes.name: observe-before-you-change
themes.description: The parent is repeatedly sent to watch and record before being asked to fix anything, and the resulting numbers are framed as a baseline rather than a grade — awareness itself is counted as progress. This is also how the book handles disappointing results: a rate, a partial win, a still-nervous child are data about the plan, not verdicts on the child. Lesson 1 assigns pure observation with no change task, Lesson 2 builds the six-step count and its non-judgmental snapshot, Lessons 3 through 7 each end in a reflection pass, and the closing reflection week asks what actually improved.

themes.name: predictability-as-kindness
themes.description: Structure is presented as comfort rather than control: a child who can see what is coming is calmer, and the schedule exists to lower anxiety, not to enforce compliance. The book keeps pairing structure with softness — calm pointing, a motivating 'then', a star that simply means today is different. Lesson 4 makes the space predictable, Lesson 5 makes the day predictable, Lesson 6 makes the tool choice predictable, Lesson 8 makes change itself predictable, and the closing overview restates the premise that children do well when their world makes sense.

themes.name: skills-must-travel
themes.description: A skill that only exists in the therapy room is not yet a skill; the book's real target is generalization across people, places and things, which is why it demands consistency between caregivers and practice in many settings. It also insists the schedule teach schedule-following with already-mastered tasks rather than smuggling in new learning. Lesson 1 names generalization as the core challenge and refuses to call the gap regression, Lesson 6 aligns the other adults, Lesson 7 stocks the bins with mastered activities, and the closing overview points onward to school, therapy and community.

themes.name: start-with-one-thing
themes.description: Against the overwhelmed parent it arrived to help, the course repeatedly refuses scale: one board, one room, one routine, one or two strategies kept for good. Narrowing is treated as the condition of anything happening at all, and the design of the site itself is justified on the same anti-overwhelm grounds. The frame rejects 'another long list of strategies', Lesson 3 picks one choice board out of a menu of fifteen, Lesson 4 picks one room and one same-day fix, Lesson 7 starts with two or three known activities, and the closing overview explicitly rejects doing everything at once or perfectly

themes.name: support-then-fade
themes.description: Help is given generously up front so the child succeeds the first time, then deliberately withdrawn a level at a time — the opposite of holding back help and correcting the error. Independence here is not something the child eventually develops but something the adult plans to stop providing. The five-level prompting hierarchy and errorless teaching arrive in Lesson 1, the seven-level version and fading are run in Lesson 4, silence and the five-second pause are the same move in Lessons 2 and 5, and Lesson 7's Independent Activity Schedule is the whole idea built into furniture.

themes.name: the-parent-is-the-intervention
themes.description: Therapy happens for an hour; the parent is there the rest of the time, so the course installs the parent as the operator — communication detective, materials-maker, librarian of the visual supports, aligner of the other caregivers. Its measure of success is a changed adult (anticipating instead of reacting) as much as a changed child. themes.name: tools-must-fit-the-child

Every catalogue it offers is immediately narrowed by a matching decision rather than adopted wholesale. themes.name: words-vanish-pictures-stay
themes.description: Speech disappears the instant it is spoken, so a child who needs processing time is being handed information that is already gone; a picture sits still and can be looked at twice. This is the mechanical justification for every tool in the course and the reason repeating yourself louder is treated as the losing move. It is argued head-on in Lesson 3 (words disappear, visuals remain; the research citations; verbal-only instructions set aside), assumed throughout Lessons 1, 2 and 4, contrasted with verbal prompting in Lesson 5, and extended to advance information in Lesson 8's social stories.
